title: e-flux Architecture—Nick Axel and Nikolaus Hirsch
description: e-flux Architecture—Nick Axel and Nikolaus Hirsch Part of the MIT Fall 2026 Architecture Lecture Series Presented with the Architecture and Urbanism Group Nikolaus Hirsch Nikolaus Hirsch is co-founder and co-editor of e-flux Architecture, as well as the director of the museum Kanal Architecture (formerly CIVA) in Brussels. He was the Dean of Städelschule and Director of the Portikus in Frankfurt and taught at the Architectural Association in London. His architectural work includes the award-winning Dresden Synagogue, Hinzert Document Center, Bockenheimer Depot Theater (with William Forsythe), Cybermohalla Hub in New-Delhi, “Do We Dream Under The Same Sky“ (with Rirkrit Tiravanija at Art Basel / LUMA Arles) and “Becoming Monument” in Fukushima. Hirsch has curated numerous exhibitions such “Wohnungsfrage / Housing Question” at the HKW in Berlin and the German Pavilion at the Architecture Biennale in Venice (“2038”). He is the editor of the Critical Spatial Practice series at Sternberg Press. Nick Axel Nick Axel is an architect, editor, educator, and curator. As Deputy Editor of e-flux Architecture, he has led the development of the platform since its founding in 2016 and undertaken more than 60 editorial projects and publications in collaboration with biennials, museums, universities, and other cultural and research institutions around the world. Nick is also Head of the Architectural Design department at the Gerrit Rietveld Academie in Amsterdam, a three-year educational program at the intersection of architecture, research, theory, and art. He was recently Editor of the 19th International Architecture Exhibition of La Biennale di Venezia, curated by Carlo Ratti, and from 2020–2022, was Curator of Architecture and Chair of the Architectural Advisory Board at the Babyn Yar Holocaust Memorial Center, Kyiv. The talk will explore architecture’s temporal dimension and its potential to address today’s challenges. The lecture follows a string of recent recognitions for the office, including the 2025 Brussels Architecture Award for Major Intervention, several nominations for the EU Mies Award, and a finalist placement, with Pierre-Antoine Gatier, in the ongoing competition to transform the Opéra Bastille in Paris. title: Joe Alterman Trio
description: Atlanta native Joe Alterman expresses a certain upbeat naivete, with a broad smile and bright eyes that make you feel welcome. One would not guess that this is a man hailed by greats; Ramsey Lewis describes his music as “happy music with tasty meat on the bones,” Les McCann states “Joe’s on a ‘blow your mind’ level,” and Ahmad Jamal calls him “a very special artist.” Journalist Nat Hentoff championed three of Alterman’s albums, as well as his writing (Joe wrote liner notes to three Wynton Marsalis/JLCO albums), calling one of Joe’s columns “one of the very best pieces on the essence of jazz, the spirit of jazz, that I’ve ever read, and I’m not exaggerating.” Joe Alterman began at NYU with a BA and Masters in Jazz Piano from NYU and has since performed at many world-renowned venues including the Kennedy Center, Lincoln Center, Birdland and Blue Note alongside Houston Person, Les McCann, Dick Gregory, Ramsey Lewis, and his own trio, among others. Downbeat describes his sound as “rooted in the blues, and with a touch reminiscent of the great pianists of the 1950s—Red Garland, Ahmad Jamal, Bill Evans.” It is clear Joe hits all of the necessary points for Jazz critics and fans alike.

title: Tap Level 2
description: Carrying on the tradition of Boston Tap, established by Maureen Cosgrove in 1976, these classes focus on developing technique, rhythm and musicality. Prior tap experience is recommended for Level 2 (Intermediate). Classes are workshop format, typically 7-week sessions. Each class will build on the weeks before, but students may join at any time if space allows. Written notation for set warm-ups are available for those who are interested. New 7-week tap session 10/29-12/17 (no class 11/26) Cost: $20 single class | 7 week session $120 *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. REGISTRATION: Email selapbailey@gmail.com Pre-registration required. Accepted Payments: Cash, Check, PayPal, Credit Card, Apple Pay (email selapbailey@gmail.com for payment information) What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Tap is an American dance form in which rhythms are audibly tapped out on the floor. It has origins in slavery and the percussive dances of West African Juba dance and Irish step dancing. It developed through minstrel shows and vaudeville in the late 19th century and emerged along with jazz in the 20th century into the art form we know today. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? Sela has been a tap teacher since 2000, taking over Maureen Cosgrove’s Boston Tap classes at the Dance Complex in 2014. While at Smith College she studied in the Five College Dance Department, performing with the Celebrations Dance Company and the UMass University Dancers. She was a founding member of the Terpsichore Ensemble in Amherst, MA and taught tap classes in Amherst and Northampton, MA before moving to Boston. Sela teaches adult beginner and intermediate tap classes at the Dance Complex, and made her Dance Complex choreographic debut at the 2018 Spring Teaching Artists and Student Concert with students from the intermediate tap class.

title: SCSB Lunch Series with Dr. Chaoyi Zhang: Reading the social brain: volumetric functional ultrasound imaging in behaving marmosets
description: Date: Friday, November 6, 2026 Time: 12:00pm – 1:00pm Location: Simons Center Conference room 46-6011. Zoom: https://mit.zoom.us/j/96729184896 Speaker: Chaoyi Zhang, Ph.D. Affiliation: Postdoctoral Fellow, Guoping Feng Laboratory, McGovern Institute for Brain Research, Yang Tan Collective, MIT Talk title: Reading the social brain: volumetric functional ultrasound imaging in behaving marmosets Abstract: Primate social brain engages distributed networks spanning prefrontal cortex, cingulate cortex, striatum, thalamus, and amygdala — circuits repeatedly implicated in autism and other neuropsychiatric disorders yet rarely observed at brain-wide scale in awake primate during genuine social interaction. The common marmoset is well suited to closing this gap: it is highly social, genetically tractable, and available as a transgenic model of autism risk genes. What has been missing is a way to record brain-wide activity while a marmoset behaves. I will present a functional ultrasound imaging (fUSI) platform we developed for awake marmosets, in which a section of skull is replaced with an acoustically transparent implant, giving volumetric access to cortical and subcortical structures at ~150 µm resolution. Combined with a marmoset whole-brain vascular reference map and an automated registration pipeline, this lets us compare activity in roughly 50 atlas-defined regions across sessions and animals. Using this platform, we find that a live social partner evokes substantially stronger and more spatially extensive activation than video of that same partner, establishing live interaction as a more powerful driver of social brain activity in this preparation. Finally, I will discuss extending this approach to transgenic marmoset models of autism, to ask which brain-wide network signatures are altered and whether they can serve as circuit-level biomarkers. title: Materials Lab Workshop: Making an Impression
description: This event is at capacity. Join assistant paper conservator Abby Schleicher and research curator Francesca Bewer for a workshop focused on art and science. You’ll discover how different printmaking techniques record both intentional design and the physical traces of making. Through hands-on experimentation using a variety of tools, pressures, inks, and papers, you’ll see how each technical choice leaves distinct traces—and why no two impressions are ever truly identical. We’ll look at a selection of prints under magnification and specialized conservation lighting to “read” their toolmarks, plate wear, inking, and condition. Linking studio experiments with close looking from a conservation perspective, this workshop will give you a concrete framework for identifying print processes and a richer appreciation of the material complexity of printed images. This workshop is one of four offered this fall that explore different media through the lens of art and science. Take one or take them all! The four workshops are: Saturday, September 19: Landscape Drawing with Optical DevicesWednesday, October 7: Color Alchemy—Pigments and DIY PaintFriday, November 6: Making an ImpressionFriday, November 20: Casting Connections—Molds, Replicas, and Questions of Authorship

title: The Need for Roots in a Digital Society | Catherine D’Ignazio
description: On November 6, Boston University’s Center for Media Innovation & Social Impact hosts its second Annual Summit. The day-long event will feature speakers, workshops, and panel discussions across disciplines and between city, university, and community members to investigate the pressing issues related to attention, ecology, community, and trust. MIT DUSP Professor Catherine D'Ignazio will be participating as a panelist during the following session on justice in the age of AI: AI systems increasingly guide decisions that play out in local contexts: who gets flagged as a risk, whose neighborhood gets patrolled or invested in, whose voice counts in a dispute. The criminal justice system is one prominent example, but the pattern recurs across many domains where data built and trained far from a community ends up shaping outcomes within it. This panel explores what it means to build systems that are answerable to the communities most affected by them. Panelists will consider what normative questions about fairness and accountability get decided, often invisibly, in technical design choices; and how local, community rooted approaches to justice can push back against technologies built at scale and at a distance. Ultimately, the question is: in the formal and informal spaces of public life, whose knowledge counts, and who gets to decide? Moderated by Kannan Thiruvengadam. The panelists include: Catherine D’Ignazio, MIT J. Nathan Matias, Cornell University Ngozi Okidegbe, Boston University

title: Bullitt
description: Directed by Peter Yates, 1968. Best known for the exhilarating and remarkably choreographed car chase that made bold and highly creative—i.e., non-geographically possible—use of actual San Francisco streets, Bullitt is in fact carefully modulated between intense bursts of action and the cool restraint embodied in Steve McQueen’s portrayal of the laconic eponymous detective. Peter Yates’ sharp eye for telling detail gives way to a crisp survey of San Francisco’s extremes, from a seedy Embarcadero flophouse hideout to a ruthlessly career-driven politician’s Pacific Heights mansion, while also offering a quieter interlude that follows McQueen shopping for TV dinners in his Nob Hill neighborhood bodega. In contrast to the rich urban texture explored throughout Bullitt are taut, extended action sequences set within institutional non-spaces—San Francisco General Hospital and the SFO International Airport—which seem to embody the tightening vice of corporate omnipresence and the rapid death of the American city described vividly by Jane Jacobs and others. Part of the series Visions of a City, Or A Weekend in San Francisco. Screening on film.

title: The Art & Science of Feathers
description: In-Person Workshop Location: The Harvard Museum of Natural History, Classroom B (Third Floor), Cambridge, MA 02138 Instructor: Erica Beade and Lorna Gibson Price: $50 members / $60 nonmembers Feathers give birds their color, from the bright red of a male Cardinal to the iridescent reds and greens of Ruby-throated Hummingbirds. Feathers keep birds warm and dry: down provides excellent insulation against heat loss, and water really does roll off a duck’s back. Feathers form the aerodynamic shape of the wing, enabling flight. A Barn Owl’s flight feathers suppress sound, allowing it to fly nearly silently, while its ruff feathers reflect and focus sound into its ears, enabling the owl to hunt in total darkness by sound alone. In this workshop, we’ll look closely at feathers through the eyes of an artist and an engineer. We’ll examine the structure of different types of feathers, see what gives feathers their color, and learn how an owl’s facial ruff feathers enable it to hunt by hearing alone. We’ll alternate between learning about feathers and exploring techniques for capturing them in pencil. All skill levels are welcome. This class is for adults. Maximum class size is 12 attendees.

description: Koo Koo is a dance party for the senses. title: Whose Landscape: The Alps Between Nation and Planet (Off-Site)
description: Through conversation and art, the afternoon invites us to reconsider the Alps not simply as a symbol of Switzerland, but as a landscape whose meaning, image, and future are shared. We will first gather at Swissnex for a panel discussion about the notion of ownership and image. As noted in the Harvard Art Museums exhibition On Location: Drawing the Outdoors, the “Swiss myth” was partially constructed by non-Swiss Romantics, such as J. M. W. Turner, John Ruskin, and Lord Byron. Two hundred and fifty years later, the same Alpine landscape is claimed at a larger scale still: as a planetary system of glaciers, biodiversity corridors, and atmospheric records that belong to no one country. Who has ever really owned the image of the Alps—and what role do cultural institutions (museums, embassies, organizations like Swissnex) play in mediating between national identity and planetary responsibility? Following the conversation, we will take a short walk to the Harvard Art Museums for an exhibition tour of On Location: Drawing the Outdoors with curators Joachim Homann and Sarah C. Rosenthal. Speakers: Claire Galloni d’Istria, Lecturer, Biologist and Visual Anthropologist, University of GenevaJoachim Homann, Maida and George Abrams Curator of Drawings, Harvard Art MuseumsAnne Whiston Spirn, Cecil and Ida Green Distinguished Professor of Landscape Architecture and Planning Professor, Massachusetts Institute of TechnologyBenji Jones (moderator), Senior Correspondent, Vox, and Nieman Fellow ’27 Funding for On Location: Drawing the Outdoors and related programming was provided by the Stanley H. Durwood Foundation Support Fund, the Stanley H. Durwood Foundation Support Fund for the Study of Dutch Drawing, the Melvin R. Seiden and Janine Luke Fund for Publications and Exhibitions, and the M. Inclusion is a priority so that all students feel welcome. Classes are “drop-in”, meaning you may join any week and there’s no “semester” commitment. Past steps are always reviewed with the introduction of 1 or 2 new steps or combos each class. Tap dancing began as an answer to the horrors of colonial enslavement…with no musical instruments, Irish and West African slaves turned to their own feet to create rhythms and percussion while pulling movement and technique from traditional tribal and cultural dances. Sounds were initially made with wooden soles, then pennies and bottle caps, finally becoming the modern metal plates screwed to the ball and heel of the shoes. These dances made their way to minstrel and vaudeville shows, eventually transforming into the broadway and rhythm style tap dancing we know today. title: Ju Dou
description: Directed by Zhang Yimou and Yang Fengliang, 1990. Singular as both an artwork and a cultural phenomenon, Ju Dou was the first Chinese film to be nominated for an Academy Award and immediately elevated international recognition of Chinese cinema, not to mention the stardom of Li Gong. Set in an early 20th century dye mill, the film is lush and operatic in its Technicolor-saturated depiction of a deadly triangle formed by a sadistic and impotent patriarch, the interloping adoptive nephew and Ju Dou the beautiful, indentured bride. Within Ju Dou ’s fiery sensuality and brutal tragedy resides moments of noir, horror, fairy tale and a rich, layered commentary on centuries of intergenerational violence. – Connor Kim ‘27 and Brittany Gravely Part of the series Nostalgia, A Harvard Undergraduate Cinematheque Program. Spotlight Tours are designed and led by Harvard undergraduates from a range of academic disciplines. Each tour is focused on objects chosen by the student and provides visitors a unique, thematic view into the collections. Tours typically feature three works of art, embrace a conversational format, and last about 45 minutes. Open to the public, these tours start outside the museum shop on Saturdays and Sundays at 11am and 2pm. This program is supported by the Ho Family Student Guide Fund. The Ho Family Student Guide Program at the Harvard Art Museums prepares students to develop original, research-based tours. Through their training, Student Guides gain knowledge of the collections and develop skills in critical thinking, visual analysis, public speaking, and leadership. Find out what the Student Guides are up to anytime on Instagram @harvardarthappens.

Unfolding like a true crime thriller, this remarkable story asks: How far is too far in the fight to do what’s right?

I was the first to teach Capoeira in New England. Mestre Joao Pequenho certified me as a teacher of Capoeira Angola in 1991. Contra Mestre Calango: I moved to Boston in 2000 to continue training with Mestre Deraldo. Since then, I traveled with him to universities and events around the world to assist in demonstrating and teaching of the beautiful art of Capoeira Angola. I graduated as a Contra Mestre in 2017. title: Fireside Chat with Rim Battal and Liza Tripp
description: Join author Rim Battal and translator Liza Tripp as they discuss the English release of Battal's novel I'll Look Myself in the Eyes! In this autobiographical coming of age novel, 17-year-old Rim is caught smoking out her window in her home in Marrakesh, Morocco. This minor transgression unleashes the fury of her mother who flies into a rage and demands that Rim complete a gynecological test certifying her virginity. So begins a nuanced journey into the tangled web of a patriarchal society in which various generations of women seem to complicitly preserve the status quo. Ultimately, it is Rim who breaks the cycle of dysfunction, rebels against tradition, confronts betrayal from the women closest to her, and dares to be her true self.

title: Donal Fox: Bearing Witness to Humanity
description: Donal Fox is internationally acclaimed as composer, pianist, and improviser in both jazz and classical music. His numerous awards include a Guggenheim fellowship in music composition, and a fellowship from the Bogliasco Foundation. He served as the first African-American composer-in-residence with the St. Louis Symphony and was a visiting artist at Harvard University, where he received a Certificate of Recognition from the President of Harvard College for his contribution to the arts. Mr. Fox premiered his Monk and Bach Project at Jazz at Lincoln Center, his orchestra piece, “Hear De Lambs A-Cyrin,” commissioned by the Albany Symphony Orchestra for The Spiritual Project at Carnegie Hall, his Scarlatti Jazz Suite Project at Ozawa Concert Hall in Tanglewood, and his piano concerto “Peace Out for Improvised Piano and Orchestra” at Carnegie Hall with the American Composers Orchestra. He has been Composer-in-Residence at Oberpfälzer Künstlerhaus (Germany), Tyrone Guthrie Centre (Ireland), Djerassi Resident Artist Program, Liguria Study Center (Italy), Tanglewood Contemporary Music Festival, among others. Donal Fox has performed and recorded with many artists including Oliver Lake, John Stubblefield, David Murray, Regina Carter, George Mraz, Al Foster, Stefon Harris, Christian Scott, Warren Wolf, Terri Lyne Carrington, Maya Beiser, Hilary Hahn, Dafnis Prieto, and poet Quincy Troupe, among others. He has recorded as composer and pianist for New World Records, Evidence Records, Music & Arts, Passin’ Thru Records, Yamaha’s Original Artist Series, Flipside Music, Steinway Spirio, and Wergo Records. His works are published by Margun Music, G. Schirmer, and Leonellis Music. He is a recipient of the prestigious American Academy of Arts and Letters Academy Award in Music and a Martin Luther King, Jr. Visiting Scholar Emeritus at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Donal Fox is a Steinway Artist.

title: Women on Trial
description: Boston Jewish Film Festival • Spotlight Screening In 1972, a landmark trial shakes France as 16-year-old Marie-Claire is prosecuted for having an illegal abortion with the help of her mother and two other defendants. In a courtroom governed by men, the verdict seems inevitable: prison for the women, while the rapist goes unpunished. Their last hope lies with Gisèle Halimi (Charlotte Gainsbourg), a fearless Jewish lawyer known for openly challenging patriarchy and confronting the system that condemns victims and lets perpetrators walk free. Alongside the accused, Gisèle will not only change their fate, but, against all odds, transform the condition of women forever. Followed by a conversation with Professor Kelly Colvin, Associate Professor of History at UMass Boston, and Professor Julian Bourg, Associate Professor of History at Boston College. Director: Lauriane Escaffre, Yvo Muller Run Time: 102 min. Release Year: 2026 Language: French with English subtitles Starring: Cécile de France, Charlotte Gainsbourg, Grégory Gadebois, Sarah Suco, Saül Benchetrit

title: Invasion of the Body Snatchers
description: Directed by Philip Kaufman, 1978. An exceptional remake of a classic that manages to equal and perhaps surpass the strengths of its predecessor, Philip Kaufman’s earthier, existential variant is set at the end of a socially and politically fraught 1970s San Francisco where “flower people” still flourish, only a more unsettling kind. A small group of radicals—including Brooke Adams’ Elizabeth and her coworker/confidant Ben played by Donald Sutherland—seem to be the only ones noticing that people are turning into uncanny shells of their former selves. The film’s horror taps into the fear of conformity, submission to authority, corporatization and a deep distrust of a government that is no longer a protector but party to the terror. Adams and Sutherland’s believable, tender portrayal of their budding romance only adds shock and heartache to a nightmare vision intensified by creepy visual details, an eerily minimal soundtrack, sophisticated special effects and disorienting camera angles. The film unnervingly envisions this painfully imaginable, always relevant, homogenizing plague for which all the usual remedies no longer exist. – Brittany Gravely Part of the series Visions of a City, Or A Weekend in San Francisco. Screening on film.

Together, we’ll slow down, awaken our senses, and experience the healing benefits of being fully present in the natural world. Through mindful walking, quiet reflection, sensory invitations, and optional moments of connection, we’ll explore how nature can help us cultivate grounding, resilience, belonging, and renewal. Surrounded by trees, birdsong, and seasonal beauty, we’ll take time to notice, breathe, and reconnect with ourselves, one another, and the more-than-human world. Whether you’re seeking calm, community, or simply a peaceful pause from everyday life, this welcoming walk offers an opportunity to restore your body, mind, and spirit while deepening your sense of connection to nature and to those walking beside you. title: RPM Fest Presents “Tom, Tom, The Piper’s Son” and others Films by Ken Jacobs
description: Run Time: 152 min. RPM Festival and the Brattle Theatre join together to pay tribute to two of experimental cinema’s most beloved and influential figures, Ken Jacobs (1933–2025) and Florence “Flo” Jacobs (née Karpf, 1941–2025). The screening honors their extraordinary artistic partnership and decades of groundbreaking work that challenged cinematic conventions and expanded the boundaries of moving-image art. A heralded filmmaker, distinguished professor at SUNY Binghamton, and defining presence in avant-garde cinema for decades, Ken Jacobs left an indelible mark on global film culture. His anarchic and uncompromising works—including BLONDE COBRA (1963), STAR SPANGLED TO DEATH (1956/2004), and the structuralist masterpiece TOM, TOM, THE PIPER’S SON (1969)—redefined how audiences experience, perceive, and understand cinema. Beginning with FLO ROUNDS A CORNER (1999), Jacobs also produced a remarkable stream of mind-bending digital videos that, in many ways, brought his artistic practice full circle to his early days as a painter. His lifelong investigation of movement, perception, texture, and the material properties of images remains central to his enduring influence. Florence Jacobs was Ken’s partner in life and an essential collaborator throughout his artistic journey. Beginning in the mid-1960s, the pair developed pioneering live-cinema and shadow-play performances that transformed film projection into an unpredictable, immersive art form. Through their double-projection “nervous system” and their “nervous magic lantern,” which conjured phantasmagorical three-dimensional images, Ken and Flo created singular, homespun spectacles that pushed the possibilities of analog film and digital cinema far beyond conventional limits. At the heart of this tribute is Ken Jacobs’s TOM, TOM, THE PIPER’S SON, a radical and enduring work that transforms a 1905 Biograph short into an essential cinematic experience. description: $20 admission / $15 for students and seniors / 1:45 doors / 2pm start New Music for the 21 piece Jazz Orchestra by resident composers David Harris, Darrell Katz, Bob Pilkington and Mimi Rabson. The Jazz Composers Alliance was founded in 41 years ago to support, develop and promote the art of music composition in the jazz idiom. The JCA Orchestra was founded to realize that goal, and it has been a fixture on Boston’s creative music scene ever since its first performance in December 1985. The JCA Orchestra has released 12 critically acclaimed CDs. Wheelworks was on Downbeat’s Best of 2016 list. The group has performed (and on a few occasions, recorded with) an illustrious group of guest performer/composers, including Sam Rivers, Julius Hemphill, Dave Holland, Maria Schneider, Henry Threadgill, Steve Lacy and Oliver Lake. Drawing on influences that span the history of jazz and the world's musical traditions, the JCA Orchestra has brought together a huge palette of sounds, structures and concepts. This group has premiered well over 125 pieces. Our concepts include extended forms, group improvisation from a variety of approaches, notated and not notated music, and striving to combine composition and improvisation in new ways. The 21-piece JCA orchestra a string trio, a vocalist, as well as a full-time flute player, and French horn, we’re not a typical big band, We have lasted since 1985, and it’s because we have a like-minded group of people who love making music, who are committed to stretching boundaries, and write and perform with joy and passion. title: Harvard Square French Fry & Pairings Food Tour
description: Harvard Square is famous for so much — Harvard University, eclectic bookshops, buskers, and a food scene that punches well above its weight. But here’s what most visitors don’t know: it’s also home to some of the best french fries in all of Massachusetts . Together with our guide Larom, a Harvard alum, we built an entire tour around that fact, and it’s become one of the most unique food experiences in Cambridge. On this 90-minute walking adventure, you’ll sample distinctly different styles of fries at three beloved Harvard Square spots — from classic hand-cut wedges to smoky BBQ fries to legendary sweet potato fries — each paired with a drink chosen specifically to bring out the flavors. We’ll try the original raspberry lime rickey , a refreshing peach lemonade , and a crazy ice cream frappe that has to be seen to be believed. All pairings are non-alcoholic, making this tour genuinely fun for the whole family. Along the way, your guide will walk you through the beloved cobblestone streets past Harvard Yard , the Widener Library , the quirky Harvard Lampoon building , and the storied Harvard Faculty Club — sharing the funny, fresh, and occasionally absurd stories that make this neighborhood unlike anywhere else in Boston. You’ll also hear the full saga of the French Fry Wars of the late 20th Century , a deliciously bizarre chapter of local food history that explains why Harvard Square’s fry scene is what it is today. This food tour is ideal for: Visitors to Boston looking for a memorable, off-the-beaten-path Cambridge experience Families with kids and teens who want something interactive and delicious Date nights — quirky, fun, and plenty of good food Birthday celebrations and small group outings Local students, grad students, alums, and neighbors who want to see a new side of Harvard!

title: Boston Manor
description: Blackpool’s Boston Manor formed in 2013 and, in two short years, worked their way to signing with renowned US indie label Pure Noise Records, worldwide. In that period, they’ve successfully built a name for themselves with their modern day emotive rock anthems and DIY work ethic. A band with expert songwriting and craftsmanship, they are also heavily involved in the production of their own videos and visual content, and as a result are now a mainstay with the likes of Kerrang TV & Scuzz. The band has also been in constant circulation across major radio stations in the UK such as BBC Radio 1 & Kerrang, with significant coverage also coming from Rock Sound, Upset & Discovered to name a few. The band were even nominated for ‘Best British Breakthrough’ at the 2018 Kerrang awards. They released their debut album ‘Be Nothing’ in 2016 to widespread acclaim and the band have continued to tour the world since then. Now veterans across the US, UK & European circuits, the band have toured with the likes of Moose Blood, Knuckle Puck, Have Mercy, Lower Than Atlantis, & Four Year Strong, and also completed a Summer on Vans Warped Tour 2017. Topping their 2017 off with high profile slots at Slam Dunk Festival, Reading & Leeds, and the Kerrang Tour, Boston Manor have stormed into 2018 fully charged, ready to unleash their next offering onto the world. Produced by Mike Sapone (Taking Back Sunday, Mayday Parade, Public Enemy), ‘Welcome To The Neighbourhood’ is a soundtrack to disenfranchisement set in a fictionalised version of the band’s hometown. In support of it’s release, the band will be heading out on their largest UK headline tour to date (including a London show at Electric Ballroom) before heading back to the US for a main support slot on the Real Friends tour to cap off an action packed 2018.

title: The Lineup
description: Directed by Don Siegel, 1958. The first of three features Don Siegel filmed in San Francisco, The Lineup uses its plot of drug smugglers racing against an almost absurdly tight deadline to trace a precise map of the city punctuated by vivid locations, including the Embarcadero YMCA and the soon-to-be destroyed Sutro Baths–each transformed into sites of baroque killings. The Lineup captures San Francisco as a port city, lingering over the harbor and a map of the bay, while also pointing to its transformation during the post-WWII years through its vivid use of ominous highway construction as a metaphor for an uncertain new order quickly leaving the old behind. Part of the series Visions of a City, Or A Weekend in San Francisco. Screening on film.

Majestic Healing Pathways™ is the foundational care model that guides all of Majestic Community Wellness’s programs. It reflects our belief that healing is a right — not a privilege — and that healing happens most sustainably when care is consistent, culturally grounded, and rooted in community. Developed in response to gaps in traditional health and wellness systems, Majestic Healing Pathways™ centers the lived experiences of Black and Brown communities who face disproportionate stress, trauma, and barriers to care. The model honors the reality that healing is not a single intervention, but a pathway built over time through breath, movement, rest, relationship, and choice. title: Jaqueline Tyrwhitt Urban Design Lecture: Dana Cuff “Coming Home: Crisis, Fire, and Recovery”
description: Dr. Dana Cuff, an educator, scholar, designer, and activist who explores how design can contribute to building more just and equitable cities, work on rebuilding after the 2025 Eaton Fire in Altadena and the housing crisis in Los Angeles. In 2006, Cuff founded cityLAB, a research and design center that initiates experimental projects to explore more equitable metropolitan possibilities. Starting in 2019, cityLAB expanded its social and political engagement by creating long term partnerships with community organizations in the region, first in the Westlake/MacArthur Park neighborhood of Los Angeles, and after the devastating fires of 2025, in Altadena. cityLAB has developed sustainable, high-performance, low-cost housing prototypes for infill sites ranging from backyards to schoolyards. Cuff will address the lab’s projects with a focus on its community-led, post-fire initiatives. Dr. Dana Cuff, a leader in urban innovation, is a Distinguished Professor at UCLA who engages spatial justice and cultural studies of architecture as a teacher, scholar, practitioner, and activist. In 2017, after a decade of research that included a full-scale demonstration house built on the UCLA campus, Cuff co-authored the first of her several pieces of California State legislation, opening 8.1M single-family lots for secondary rental units. In 2024, she launched “Small Lots, Big Impacts,” a design-development initiative to build a new generation of dense, compact starter homes on publicly-held land. Cuff has authored numerous books, includingArchitectures of Spatial Justice(MIT Press, 2023),Urban Humanities: New Practices for Reimagining the City(MIT Press, 2020),Architects’ People(with W.R. Ellis; 1989), andArchitecture: The Story of Practice(1989).

description: Classes teach Broadway style tap and focus on repetitive technique to encourage muscle memory and the confidence to create clear sounds. Inclusion is a priority so that all students feel welcome. Classes are “drop-in”, meaning you may join any week and there’s no “semester” commitment. Accepted Payments: Cash, Venmo (@christina-harrington-7) What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Tap dancing began as an answer to the horrors of colonial enslavement…with no musical instruments, Irish and West African slaves turned to their own feet to create rhythms and percussion while pulling movement and technique from traditional tribal and cultural dances. Sounds were initially made with wooden soles, then pennies and bottle caps, finally becoming the modern metal plates screwed to the ball and heel of the shoes. These dances made their way to minstrel and vaudeville shows, eventually transforming into the broadway and rhythm style tap dancing we know today. As a child she studied tap, jazz, and ballet at the Paula Coffey Dance Center in East Bridgewater, MA from 1987-1995 where tap was always her favorite. title: Vertigo
description: Directed by Alfred Hitchcock, 1958. Hitchcock’s grand enigma was recently enshrined as the greatest film of all time in the British Film Institute’s respected survey, infamously displacing Citizen Kane for the first time in fifty years. A tantalizing spiral into the abyss, the film follows Scottie Ferguson, an ex-police detective in forced retirement after his last case ended in a tragic death, as he is enlisted as a private investigator to keep an eye on an old friend’s wife. Following Madeleine, he is drawn into a sprawling riddle of love and death, from which he may never emerge. This is Hitchcock’s most profound and troubling exploration of his persistent themes: doppelgängers and duality, obsession, women trapped by deceit and the inexorable destructiveness of male desire. A cinematic landmark, Vertigo retains its power as a perplexing and harrowing nightmare. – Jason Michelitch Part of the series Visions of a City, Or A Weekend in San Francisco. Screening on film.

Across multiple critically acclaimed, Grammy nominated albums, Hiss Golden Messenger has become known for its warmth and emotional clarity, as well as Taylor’s ability to connect the personal and poetic with the political without losing intimacy or musical grace. description: $15 @ the door / $10 students / 8:30 start / 8pm doors / seated Jerry Bergonzi , Tenor Saxophone Luther Gray , Drums Plamen Karadonev, Piano Sean Farias, Bass Special Guest , Trumpet A fine, high-powered tenor saxophonist with a tone influenced by John Coltrane, a mastery of chord changes, and a strong musical imagination, Jerry Bergonzi has long had an underground following in the Boston area. He started on clarinet when he was eight, switching to alto at 12, and finally to tenor two years later. Bergonzi was inspired early on by Sonny Rollins, Coltrane, and Hank Mobley. He attended Lowell University and then after graduation played electric bass in local bands behind singers and strippers, saving up enough money to move to New York in 1972. After struggling in the Big Apple for seven years and gaining some recognition as a member of Two Generations of Brubeck and of the Dave Brubeck Quartet (with whom he appeared on several Concord albums during 1979-1981), Bergonzi moved back to Boston in 1981, where he developed a strong career both as a tenorman and as an educator. He has since led several groups (including two called Con Brio and Gonz) and recorded for the Plug, Not Fat, Red, and Blue Note labels. — By Scott Yanow, AllMusic Continuing Every Monday at 8:30pm Lineup subject to change

description: Time: 3:00 - 4:00pm Speaker: Ziyang Gao (UCLA) Title: Towards uniformity in rational torsion and small points on abelian varieties Abstract: On an elliptic curve E defined over a number field K, a celebrated theorem of Mazur, Kamienney, and Merel asserts the number of its rational torsion points is bounded above solely in terms of the degree of K — known as the uniform boundedness conjecture for elliptic curves. On the other hand, the Lang-Silverman conjecture predicts that the height of non-torsion rational points, divided by the Faltings height of E, is bounded below uniformly in terms of K. In this talk, I will present a different method (inspired by Vojta's proof of the Mordell Conjecture) to study both conjectures for abelian varieties of arbitrary dimension. Over number fields, we prove both conjectures assuming a suitable generalized version of Szpiro's conjecture. Over function fields of characteristic 0, we resolve both conjectures unconditionally, giving a new proof of a remarkable result of Looper and Yap earlier this year — a common key ingredient is Deligne's Arakelov Inequality. The bound obtained by our method is explicit and depends polynomially on the base field. We also prove both conjectures for elliptic curves over function fields of characteristic p. Joint work with Kaiyuan Gu. ------------------------------------------------------------ Time: 4:30 - 5:30pm Speaker: Daniel Litt (University of Toronto) Title: The arithmetic of differential equations Abstract: In 1875 Fuchs asked for a criterion that determines when the solutions to an algebraic differential equation are themselves algebraic functions. Conjectural answers to this question have been given by Grothendieck and Katz, Ekedahl--Shepherd-Barron--Taylor, and Bost, in terms of the arithmetic of the differential equation's structure constants. title: McGovern Institute Special Seminar with Alan Mardinly & Murat Günel
description: Seminar with Alan Mardinly & Murat Günel Date: Tuesday, November 10, 2026Time: 3:00pmLocation: Seminar Room 3189, Building 46This is an in-person event Talk Title: Towards dopaminergic biohybrid implants for Parkinson's disease Abstract: Neural interfaces traditionally stimulate the brain with electric fields, but the brain mostly talks to itself using chemical neurotransmitters. Optogenetics approaches to brain modulations are widespread in research, but have not translated to the clinic because of challenges in opsin sensitivity, gene delivery, and immunogenicity. However, allogeneic cell therapies have recently made the jump to the clinic. Here, we describe an approach to neural interfacing leveraging these advances to combine optogenetics with immune-evasive cell therapy. First we developed an ultrasensitve microbial opsin using modern protein language models and high throughput patch clamp screening. Then we engineered the genome of iPSCs to express the opsin and evade the immune system, and show that they fail to elicit an immune response in humanized mice. We differentiated these iPSC into midbrain dopamine neuron progenitors and engraft the cells in a thin-film micro-LED implant, and demonstrate rescue of a mouse model of Parkinson's disease. Additionally, we explore the applications of this technology for a high bandwidth general purpose cortical BCI. Together these advances define a new therapeutic modality in which engrafted cells and be controlled by a neuromodulatory device, allowing us to direct the spatiotemporal release of specific neurotransmitters in the brain for therapeutic applications. title: SCSB Special Seminar with Dr. Aya Ito-Ishida: Cross-species analyses reveal conserved cortical network alterations in Rett syndrome
description: Date: Tuesday, November 10, 2026 Location: 46-3002 (Singleton Auditorium). Please note this talk will not be recorded Time: 4:00pm-5:00pm ET Speaker: Aya Ito-Ishida, M.D., Ph.D. Affiliation: Team Director, Laboratory for Brain Development and Disorders, RIKEN Center for Brain Science Hosts: Dr. Giselle Fernandes, Dr. Mriganka Sur Talk title: Cross-species analyses reveal conserved cortical network alterations in Rett syndrome Abstract: Cortical circuits undergo extensive reorganization during development to support the emergence of complex cognitive behaviors. Disruption of this process is thought to contribute to neurodevelopmental disorders, but how genetic alterations reshape large-scale cortical organization, how these changes relate to behavioral impairments, and whether they can be reversed remain poorly understood. Rett syndrome, a monogenic neurodevelopmental disorder, provides a unique genetically defined system for linking molecular alterations, large-scale circuit dysfunction, and behavioral consequences. In this talk, I will present our recent work combining resting-state fMRI in individuals with Rett syndrome and wide-field calcium imaging in mice. Our findings suggest a conserved disruption of cortical functional hierarchy that is closely associated with behavioral severity. Furthermore, we find that this abnormality is reversible following MECP2 reintroduction in mice, suggesting that this approach may provide a cross-species framework for evaluating emerging therapies in Rett syndrome and related neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: 115 Sycamore School Building Project Community Forum
description: The City is planning to build a new school at 115 Sycamore Street. All community members are invited to come learn more about the project and share their perspectives at an upcoming community forum: Time and Date: Tuesday, November 10, from 6 to 8 p.m. Location: Somerville High School, Highlander Forum, 81 Highland Avenue During this meeting Mayor Wilson and Superintendent Carmona will speak to the City and District’s shared vision for the project, which is informed both by community process as well as district needs. Project architects, Perkins Eastman, will then present the preferred design option for the project, which was submitted to the state in late August --providing an overview of how the building will support the diverse learning needs of Somerville’s students and incorporate a range of community priorities into the design. title: The Bowery Presents Pokey LaFarge
description: Pokey LaFarge is coming to Arts at the Armory on November 10, 2026 to celebrate the release of his new album, 'Rent Money'. Grab your tickets now! Get Your Tickets! For two decades, Pokey LaFarge has walked his own effortlessly cool road as an exceptionally iconoclastic troubadour – forthright, genuine, and markedly keen to put it all out there. Rent Money now sees him pushing forward yet again in what can be safely declared his finest collection to date, both as an heartfelt expression of personal experience and as no-nonsense social commentary. With its twanging guitars, plucky rhythms, and undeniably captivating melodies, the album soars and swings, its joyous refrains belying the inescapable undercurrent of constant worry and angst that permeates these troubled times. As always, the Illinois native deftly traverses the genre boundaries, seamlessly integrating the myriad strains of 20th-century American music with a freewheeling command of earnest songcraft, inspired performance, and subversive creativity. Rent Money stands tall as an indisputable high-water mark for Pokey LaFarge – a defining collection from a one-of-a-kind artist of rare ingenuity and uncommon candor, now as ever, determinedly crafting a sure-footed brand of deeply human music all his own. title: the olllam
description: With a name aptly deriving from the old Irish for a grand master of a skill, the olllam is a Transatlantic collective of formidable talent, marrying stunning instrumental virtuosity, Irish tradition, and Detroit’s post-rock psych-sensibility. Their genre-defying compositions are lush with cyclical trance-like melodies, co-written by Belfast uilleann piper/whistle player John McSherry, his US protégé Tyler Duncan, and master-drummer Michael Shimmin, whose intricate, often complex, rhythms are then underpinned in recording by the phenomenal bass-playing genius of Joe Dart (Vulfpeck, Fearless Flyers.) Their 2012 eponymous debut album is now considered something of a cult classic, winning the 2012 Indie Acoustic Music Award for Best Instrumental Album. Over the years the olllam has toured as a live collective augmented by additional master musicians and collaborators, including Dart’s Vulfpeck bandmates Theo Katzman and Woody Goss. Since the recording and release of 2022’s long-awaited follow-up album elllegy , which saw the olllam named as RTE Radio Best Group at that year’s Folk Awards, the band has featured Limerick’s Seán O’Meara on guitar and Detroit producer Joe Hettinga on keys. In 2024 Scottish whistle-player and piper Ross Ainslie joined the olllam, as Tyler decided to focus on his career as a producer. A hugely successful tour of UK and Ireland followed, including sell out shows at Glasgow Barrowlands and London Jazz Cafe, and a collaboration with Zedd on his August 2024 album, Telos .

description: Attend one of our most beloved, longest standing brewery traditions: Trivia Tuesday! Every Tuesday swing by our Broadway taproom for our weekly trivia night. It’s free to compete, and winners get beer money. Here’s how it works: show up with your team of 2 – 6 players starting at 7:00 pm, when we’ll open the doors to the back taproom. Head down the hallway to the back, then snag a seat. All seating is first come first serve, so we recommend arriving early – there generally is a line! Questions rotate every week, and cover categories ranging from history, politics, sports, movies, pop culture, music, and more. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? My kathak journey began with Gretchen Hayden, Founder of Chhandika Boston and Senior Disciple of Pandit Chitresh Das. Pandit Das was the pioneer of kathak dance bringing his rich training and upbringing in Kolkata, India to the US in 1971. Ballet originated in the Italian Renaissance courts around 1500 as large balls or spectacles that were performed by members of the royal court. The French king, Louis XIV, created the first academy and the positions, steps, and movements of the ballet were collected and codified. The spectacles began to be performed by artists that were trained in the academy, originally as part of an opera, and later as ballets that told a story through music, mime, and dance. Over the centuries ballet has influenced folk dance styles of many (mainly European) nations and, more recently, has been influenced by folk, modern, and contemporary forms of dance from all countries. title: Richard P. Stanley Seminar in Combinatorics
description: Speaker: Lang Mou (UC Davis) Title: Leafy trees, wall-crossing, and m-Tamari intervals Abstract: Trees appear in several approaches to wall-crossing. I will present a new plane-tree model for the central wall in rank-2 cluster scattering diagrams, inspired by the recently introduced tight gradings on Dyck paths. These trees turn out to be in bijection with intervals in the m-Tamari lattice, a lattice on m-ballot paths. I will explain this correspondence and show how the tree perspective leads to algebraic functional equations for enumerating these intervals and a new combinatorial proof of the central wall formula. No prior knowledge of wall-crossing or cluster algebras will be assumed. This talk is based on joint work with Amanda Burcroff and Kyungyong Lee.

Linear Salsa is a hybrid dance that comes from Mambo (a Cuban style that was popularized in the 1950’s NYC Palladium). NY Mambo is a marriage of footwork and partner-work from Cuba (Aftro-Cuban movements, Cuban Son) and the U.S. (Jazz, Swing). Salsa is a marketing term popularized in the 1970’s to commodify all Latin music and dance to a U.S. audience. Circular Salsa primarily comes from the Cuban dance Casino, which itself originates from Cuban Son. Salsa is by nature transformational, multinational, and multigenerational, embodying the shared heritage of Latin music. title: Live Blues & Roots Music Returns to Harvard Square: Wednesday Nights @ The Sea Hag Restaurant & Bar
description: The Sea Hag Restaurant & Bar and The Barrett Anderson Band are excited to announce a new weekly series, Blues & Roots Wednesdays , bringing live music back home to historic Harvard Square. “Cambridge, our fair city, and I share deep roots, and I’m thrilled to find a new musical home at The Sea Hag,” says Massachusetts-based singer/guitarist, Barrett Anderson. “Good music and good food are two of our most basic, fundamental needs,” he continues, “What great joy they give us. I am so happy to revel in that every Wednesday night with my dearest musical friends, and Kari and her incredible team at The Sea Hag. We go way back together, and I can’t imagine all the fun we have ahead.” Indeed, Anderson has strong connections to this scene. He remembers: “My first professional experience came when I was 15, backing up Muddy Waters’ band alums Pinetop Perkins and Bob Margolin at the original House of Blues on Winthrop Street. A few months after that I began busking, you’d often find me in Brattle Square or by the pit. This would have been mid/late 90s.” While still a teen, Anderson was a member of The Monster Mike Welch Band and Ronnie Earl & The Broadcasters (“Ronnie was my guitar hero. Then he was my teacher, then my boss. Now he’s my musical Father,” Anderson says), before eventually starting The Barrett Anderson Band in 2007. Anderson won a Boston Music Award (2013 Blues Artist of the Year), was on the Billboard charts (2020’s live album Hynoboogie spent 3 weeks on the Billboard Blues Album chart, peaking at #6), and was nominated for a Blues Music Award (2023 Band of the Year with Anthony Geraci & The Boston Blues All-Stars), all the while playing nationally, internationally, and locally in Cambridge and the greater Boston area. In addition to the musical roots, long-time locals may recognize Anderson from a decade serving tables and bartending at The Sea Hag’s sister establishment, Grendel’s Den, or from Abodeon, the mid-century modern shop started by his family. title: The Bad Plus
description: This is the farewell tour of The Bad Plus — the last chance to see them live. For over two decades, The Bad Plus have been one of the most influential and distinctive formations in modern jazz. The American band came to international attention in the early 2000s and quickly built a reputation for opening jazz to new audiences with complete musical conviction — uncompromising, stylistically open, and full of enormous energy. The group became famous for their radical reinterpretations of rock and pop songs as well as for their original compositions. Over the course of their career, The Bad Plus released numerous acclaimed albums on labels including Columbia Records and Nonesuch, and collaborated with artists such as Joshua Redman, Wendy Lewis, and Bill Frisell. 2026 marks the end of an era: the band has announced they will dissolve after their current tour. That makes this an especially rare opportunity to experience one of the defining groups of modern jazz one final time. Between complex structures, improvisational openness and enormous rhythmic precision, The Bad Plus have left a lasting mark on the sound of contemporary jazz.

description: Based on the true story of Katherine Ann Power and Clare Schroeder, this gripping new drama follows two women bound by a single, life-altering moment. It’s 1970. title: AI and Climate Change: Modeling the Future with En-ROADS / Sustainability Lunch Series
description: Questions about artificial intelligence (AI) arise in almost every climate change conversation. How much electricity will data centers need? What is the impact of AI on the climate? Will AI help or hurt efforts to cut emissions? In this Sustainability Lunch Series Session, MIT Professor John Sterman will dive deep into the latest update to the En-ROADS Climate Solutions Simulator, which lets you explore the interconnectedness of AI, energy, emissions, and the economy. Attendees will learn how and why data centers contribute to energy demand and emissions, as well as the indirect effects of scaling AI and why they may outweigh the direct footprint of data centers. You’ll leave ready to explore the AI and data center sector in En-ROADS and lead your own conversations using the simulator. Food Provided

title: Frances Loeb Library Faculty Author Talks: Ana María Leon in Conversation with Fernando Luis Martínez Nespral “A History of the Arab Component in Ibero-American Architecture”
description: Hosted by the Frances Loeb Library at the Harvard Graduate School of Design, Faculty Author Talks provide a venue for GSD faculty members to launch newly published books, discuss recent or in-process publications or research in which they are currently engaged, or present their thoughts on pedagogy and innovative approaches to teaching. Please join in the library for a conversation between Ana María Leon and Fernando Luis Martínez Nespral on the recent publication, a History of the Arab Component in Ibero-American Architecture, published byBrill. Fernando Luis Martínez Nespralis an architect (Universidad de Buenos Aires) with a PhD in History from Universidad Torcuato Di Tella. He is Full Professor of Architectural History and Director of the Instituto de Arte Americano e Investigaciones Estéticas at the School of Architecture, Design, and Urbanism, UBA, where he also edits the journal Anales del IAA. His work explores Islamic architecture and its connections with the Ibero-American world, most recently in A History of the Arab Component in Iberoamerican Architecture (Brill, 2026), along with numerous publications in English and Spanish. He is a member of several international networks, including the Society of Architectural Historians, the Global Architectural History Teaching Collaborative, and Our North is the South, which he co-founded. Ana María León’swork traces how spatial practices and transnational networks of power and resistance shape the modernity and coloniality of the Americas. Her research and teaching foregrounds the agency of populations under struggle and the multiple forms of bias embedded in the built environment and its histories. León is invested in collaborative approaches to learning, teaching, and writing. Attention to multiple critical positions, particularly those of historically underrepresented groups, she argues, grounds our understanding of history in the politics of coliberation. Karen Korellis Reuther with Dean Sarah Whiting and Prof

She got her Ph.D. from Princeton University (2004), writing a thesis on Iraqi intellectual history under the supervision of Professors Robert Tignor and Samah Selim, and her BA (1995) and MA (1999) from Tel Aviv University. title: Harvard Square French Fry & Pairings Food Tour
description: Harvard Square is famous for so much — Harvard University, eclectic bookshops, buskers, and a food scene that punches well above its weight. But here’s what most visitors don’t know: it’s also home to some of the best french fries in all of Massachusetts . Together with our guide Larom, a Harvard alum, we built an entire tour around that fact, and it’s become one of the most unique food experiences in Cambridge. On this 90-minute walking adventure, you’ll sample distinctly different styles of fries at three beloved Harvard Square spots — from classic hand-cut wedges to smoky BBQ fries to legendary sweet potato fries — each paired with a drink chosen specifically to bring out the flavors. We’ll try the original raspberry lime rickey , a refreshing peach lemonade , and a crazy ice cream frappe that has to be seen to be believed. All pairings are non-alcoholic, making this tour genuinely fun for the whole family. Along the way, your guide will walk you through the beloved cobblestone streets past Harvard Yard , the Widener Library , the quirky Harvard Lampoon building , and the storied Harvard Faculty Club — sharing the funny, fresh, and occasionally absurd stories that make this neighborhood unlike anywhere else in Boston. You’ll also hear the full saga of the French Fry Wars of the late 20th Century , a deliciously bizarre chapter of local food history that explains why Harvard Square’s fry scene is what it is today. This food tour is ideal for: Visitors to Boston looking for a memorable, off-the-beaten-path Cambridge experience Families with kids and teens who want something interactive and delicious Date nights — quirky, fun, and plenty of good food Birthday celebrations and small group outings Local students, grad students, alums, and neighbors who want to see a new side of Harvard!

title: Au: Origins Unearthed
description: Register for In-Person Register for Online A new Exhibit Spotlight, Au: Origins Unearthed , in the Earth & Planetary Sciences Gallery of the Harvard Museum of Natural History, examines the global impacts of gold extraction—from illegal artisanal mining and mercury contamination to emerging efforts to promote traceability and responsible sourcing. This interdisciplinary program opens with a look at scientific research on mercury contamination caused by illegal gold mining in Amazonian rivers, exploring its effects on Indigenous communities, waterways, soils, and forests. A panel discussion will follow, featuring jewelry designers, activists, and legal experts working in Colombia, Brazil, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Together, they will consider pathways toward more ethical and responsible mining, systems that enable companies and consumers to trace gold to its source, and tools for identifying illegal mining. A reception will follow in the Earth & Planetary Sciences Gallery of the Harvard Museum of Natural History. Free event parking is available with registration. Register by November 11 to receive parking registration instructions. Lecture by Elsie M. Sunderland, Fred Kavli Professor of Environmental Chemistry and Professor of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Harvard University Followed by a panel discussion with Ariene Bomfim Cerqueira , Conservation Specialist, World Wildlife Fund-Brazil Ashley Alexis McFarlane , Jewelry Designer and Founder, Omi Woods Erich Adam Moreira Lima , Federal Criminal Forensic Expert and Head of the Forensic Geology Service, Brazilian Federal Police Program moderated by journalist Melanie Grant and Raquel Alonso-Perez , curator of the Mineralogical and Geological Museum, Harvard University.

She has been a faculty member at the Faculty of Architecture at UNAM since 2003, where she currently directs the RX Studio Research and Degree Seminar. She has taught at the Harvard Graduate School of Design, Kent State University, and the WAVE program in Venice, Italy, among others. Her work has been exhibited and awarded at numerous national and international biennials and published in national and international media such as Domus, Casabella, Arquitectura Viva, and The Architectural Review, among others. title: Hiawatha Performances and the Garden River First Nation
description: In August of 1900, several members of the Longfellow family travelled to Desbarats, Ontario, where they had been invited to attend the first performance of Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s poem Hiawatha put on by members of the Garden River First Nation. These productions, which spread throughout Indigenous communities across Western Ontario and Northern Michigan in the years that followed, featured largely Native actors and were performed in the Anishinaabe language. Analyzing these Hiawatha performances offers a window to explore how Native people reappropriated Western representations to insist on the survival of their own peoples and traditions. This event will feature two talks about the August 1900 performance based on research done in the collections held by the Longfellow House-Washington’s Headquarters’ National Historic Site. The first, by Professor Karl Hele, will describe the context and circumstances of the performance. The second, by Professor Alan Corbiere, will look at the use of the Anishinaabe language in the performances and in the material created for the Longfellow family. Alan Corbiere, Bne wedoodemid (Ruffed Grouse clan), is an Anishinaabe from M'Chigeeng First Nation on Manitoulin Island. He is an assistant professor of history and Canada Research Chair in Indigenous History of North America at York University. His research focuses on Anishinaabe language, oral traditions, and material culture. He has published in the journals Museum Anthropology, the Algonquian Papers, and others, as well as in the edited collection Afterlives of Indigenous Archives: Essays in Honor of the Occom Circle. He has also served as the the Executive Director at the Ojibwe Cultural Foundation and the Anishinaabemowin Revitalization Program Coordinator at Lakeview School, both in M’Chigeeng First Nation. Karl S. Hele, a member of Garden River First Nation, is a full professor and current Director of Canadian and Indigenous Studies at Mount Allison University in Sackvi

title: Carlson Lecture — The Ocean Carbon Sink: Facts, Fictions, and Opportunities
description: The Lorenz Center is pleased to present the 2026 John H. Carlson Lecture, in partnership with the New England Aquarium and the Lowell Institute. FEATURING Dr. Marina Lévy Oceanographer and Senior Scientist at the French National Centre for Scientific Research, LOCEAN–IPSL Sorbonne Université Can whales help mitigate human-induced climate change? What about mangroves, kelp forests, or the trillions of microscopic organisms drifting through the ocean and capturing carbon through photosynthesis? The ocean absorbs about a quarter of the CO₂ we emit, so it seems natural to imagine that ocean life is doing the work much as forests do on land. But the real story is more complex. Join oceanographer Marina Lévy on an exploration of the ocean’s extraordinary carbon machine. From forests on land to underwater forests, from microscopic phytoplankton to the web of marine life and the global ocean circulation, we will follow carbon through the ocean to discover what actually makes it one of the planet’s great carbon sinks and why that matters as the ocean warms and its circulation changes. And if we understand how this remarkable machine works, could we help it absorb even more CO₂? We will explore some of the emerging ideas for using the ocean to remove carbon from the atmosphere, along with their promises, limitations, and unanswered questions. In person at the Simons Theatre, Central Wharf, Boston – OR – via live stream with pre-registration. Free and open to the public. Students and families welcome.Doors open at 5:30 with exhibits from MIT students and climate scientists in the Simons Theatre lobby. Register by November 11 ABOUT OUR SPEAKER Dr. Marina Lévy is an oceanographer and senior scientist at the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS), based at LOCEAN–IPSL at Sorbonne University in Paris, France. title: Infrastructure in a Time of Flux: Methods, Conditions, and Situations Symposium
description: Infrastructure in a Time of Fluxforegrounds a body of architectural, engineering, urban planning, and design innovations whose potential remains largely unrealized in these contexts. Bringing together historical precedents and contemporary investigations, the exhibition examines lightweight, adaptable, deployable, and materially efficient building methods while asking why their broader social and design applications remain elusive. The symposium, like theexhibition on view in Druker Design Gallery, poses a critical question: if architecture has produced such sophisticated methods for building with fewer resources, greater adaptability, and increased efficiency, why have these innovations rarely been directed toward the conditions that constitute the lived reality of a large portion of humanity? In reconsidering this question, we invite a broader reflection on the relationship between invention and implement-ation, and on the capacity of design disciplines to engage with a world defined not by permanence but by flux. title: Jake Klar with Noble Dust & Hayley Sabella
description: Jake Klar with Noble Dust & Hayley Sabella Join us at The Rockwell for a curated evening of Folk Rock and Alt-Country, celebrating Jake Klar’s album release, with special guests Noble Dust and Hayley Sabella. ABOUT JAKE KLAR: Years Go Through Me Now , a new collaborative album by singer-songwriter Jake Klar and folk-rock trio Blue Ranger, is a quiet triumph of such glimpses. In its nine songs and two interludes, I hear the motions of weathered hands, the gentle rush of country roads, the laughter of old friends and the silence of rumination — the quilt of dreams and doings we call a life. GoldFlakePaint describes Klar’s music as “An urgent meeting of folk, roots and good old rock and roll that carries with it an unbreakable spirit.” A fixture in New England’s folk scene, Klar has toured nationally, played festivals including Otis Mountain Get Down and FreshGrass, and supported the likes of Cut Worms, Antwaun Stanley, and Al Olender. Klar has spent the past decade working as a letterpress printer, art store clerk, bartender, carpenter, illustrator, graphic designer, musician (touring DIY on his own and as a member of Prewn and Hannah Mohan), live sound engineer, merch guy, and custodian. His songwriting, from the misty-eyed title track to the down-home boogie-woogie of “Driving Home Through the Country” (here recast murmurously from an earlier electric version), dwells in a rustic realm borne by his crackling voice and hearthside acoustic guitar. “That Forever” is a haunted, fragmented road-movie that emerges from its dust like a lost Basement Tapes recording, while the last-call piano ballad “Louisa” wouldn’t sound amiss on After The Gold Rush . Tap is an American dance form in which rhythms are audibly tapped out on the floor. It has origins in slavery and the percussive dances of West African Juba dance and Irish step dancing. It developed through minstrel shows and vaudeville in the late 19th century and emerged along with jazz in the 20th century into the art form we know today. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? Sela has been a tap teacher since 2000, taking over Maureen Cosgrove’s Boston Tap classes at the Dance Complex in 2014. While at Smith College she studied in the Five College Dance Department, performing with the Celebrations Dance Company and the UMass University Dancers. She was a founding member of the Terpsichore Ensemble in Amherst, MA and taught tap classes in Amherst and Northampton, MA before moving to Boston. Sela teaches adult beginner and intermediate tap classes at the Dance Complex, and made her Dance Complex choreographic debut at the 2018 Spring Teaching Artists and Student Concert with students from the intermediate tap class.

title: Sleep at The Sinclair
description: Today, the legendary band Sleep releases new single “ Have Spacesuit Will Travel ” via Third Man Records , their first new music since 2018. In addition, the band announces a fall North American tour , as well as releases the first issue of the Sleep Comic Book , written by bassist and songwriter Al Cisneros . “Have Spacesuit Will Travel” begins Sleep’s first mission without Matt Pike on guitar. The music and art are alive and after the decades of obstacles that Sleep has overcome, it is time to move forward and make songs and albums. Al wishes Matt the best on his earth bound maneuvers. Alongside Cisneros, the latest incarnation of Sleep features Dale Crover on drums and Bubba Dupree on guitar. Dale has been in some serious bands, like the Melvins and Redd Kross . That Al would seek him out makes sense, an almost elementary choice that probably wouldn’t raise too many eyebrows. Bubba Dupree, from the fiercely loved band Void , hailing out of Columbia, MD, is a pick that is not only completely mind-blowing, but a choice no one would have seen coming. Just the thought of Bubba, who was amazing from the first Void shows on, playing guitar in Sleep is almost too much for the mind to comprehend. Al Cisneros, Bubba Dupree, and Dale Crover as a trio looks really good on paper, but the only way to see if it worked was to get everyone in a room and play. Al says the answer made itself evident immediately: “The vibe of the first jam was obvious. It was blue sunglasses-era Iommi in the quality, and equally awesome is Bubba is also one of the coolest people I’ve been able to make music with.” “Have Spacesuit Will Travel” at no time tries to pick up where The Sciences left off. There’s a considerable amount of new blood in the band, so imitation, as Bubba notes, would greatly limit the potential of three very unique and talented musicians. The symposium, like theexhibition on view in Druker Design Gallery, poses a critical question: if architecture has produced such sophisticated methods for building with fewer resources, greater adaptability, and increased efficiency, why have these innovations rarely been directed toward the conditions that constitute the lived reality of a large portion of humanity? title: Infinite-Dimensional Algebra Seminar
description: Speaker: Tudor Pădurariu (University of Bonn​​​​​​​) Title: Abelian quasi-BPS categories Abstract: I will report on joint work in progress with Sabin Cautis and Yukinobu Toda. The Grothendieck group of the Hall category of a quiver is isomorphic to a positive half of the quantum affine algebra corresponding to the quiver. We show that two structures on the Hall category are compatible: a perverse coherent t-structure and a filtration by window categories. In particular, we construct t-structures on the so-called quasi-BPS categories, which generate Hall categories. We thus obtain a refinement of the total BPS cohomology of the quiver, whose dimension is the value at one of the Kac polynomial of the quiver, in terms of nilpotent orbits. I will discuss examples of quasi-BPS categories for finite-type quivers, where they may be compared with categories of representations of KLR algebras, and for the Jordan quiver. As a corollary, we prove a conjecture of Gorsky–Negut about generators of the category of coherent sheaves on the commuting stack. Zoom: https://mit.zoom.us/j/91800438944. For the Passcode, please contact Pavel Etingof at etingof@math.mit.edu. Note: the seminar will run on occasion throughout this Fall semester.

title: SHOWCASE: Community Engagement & Participatory Design
description: A public showcase in conjunction with the Forum on Community Engagement and Participatory Design in Humanitarian Innovation and Disaster Response. A public showcase of posters and project displays from participants in the Forum on Community Engagement and Participatory Design in Humanitarian Innovation and Disaster Response, as well as from students, faculty, and organizations engaged in this work. Light refreshments will be served. Background Humanitarian crises are growing in scale and frequency, while at the same time, funding and other resources for humanitarian aid are shrinking. Humanitarian innovation strives to help close that gap by designing and developing new and more effective aid products, processes, and programs. The scarcity of resources makes it increasingly important to ensure that these innovations are culturally and contextually appropriate to maximize their effectiveness and efficiency. Since the World Humanitarian Summit in 2016, there has been growing emphasis on the importance of increasing participation of the affected population in humanitarian solutions. This moment makes finding practical pathways to do so even more urgent. The convergence of several different but related disciplines can catalyze new ways to bring people affected by crisis into the design of innovations in humanitarian response, disaster preparedness, and risk reduction. The Forum and Showcase bring together actors from design, humanitarian innovation, urban risk reduction, humanitarian response, community engagement, disaster response, and disaster preparedness to explore ways for increasing community participation in innovations in humanitarian and disaster response. Sponsored by MIT D-Lab, the MIT Urban Risk Lab, Boston University's Center on Forced Displacement, Red Social Innovation, the Japanese Red Cross College of Nursing Disaster Management Research Institute, the Japanese Red Cross Academy, and MIT MAD.

title: World Class Music Live Presents Rumbo Tumba

Rumbo Tumba is a craftsman of organic loops, performing, recording, and mixing a variety of handcrafted South American instruments in real time. The live show features an impressive array of wooden instruments with which he constructs a unique natural sound and an atmosphere that transports listeners to the purest places in nature. Loop-based compositions highlight the beauty of traditional folk roots and delicately employ cutting-edge digital tools to project South American folklore into the future. title: The X-Tet Sounds of Italy
description: The X-tet returns with a sweeping celebration of Italian Baroque and Renaissance music , joined by GRAMMY® award-winning soprano Amanda Forsythe and viola da gamba player Cristiano Contadin . Spanning four centuries of Italy’s most treasured chamber repertoire, the ensemble brings to life virtuosic works by Vivaldi, Albinoni, Castello, and Handel alongside rarely heard gems by Maria Teresa Agnesi and Antonio Archilei. Highlights include Handel’s dramatic cantata “Armida abbandonata” and Archilei’s celestial “Dalle più alte sfere,” both featuring Forsythe’s celebrated voice, alongside instrumental showpieces for strings, theorbo, and harpsichord. The program concludes with a nod to folk tradition in the spirited Tarantella Gargano, before Colin Jacobsen’s new work , Morgantina Studies, brings the evening to a close. Dates/Times Friday, November 13, 2026 | 7:30 PM Saturday, November 14, 2026 | 7:30 PM Estimated Run Time 90 MIN | No Intermission Location Boston Conservatory at Berklee, Seully Hall | 8 Fenway, Boston, MA 02215 Ticket Prices $30 – $70

Through mindful walking, quiet reflection, sensory invitations, and optional moments of connection, we’ll explore how nature can help us cultivate grounding, resilience, belonging, and renewal. Surrounded by trees, birdsong, and seasonal beauty, we’ll take time to notice, breathe, and reconnect with ourselves, one another, and the more-than-human world. title: Spotlight Tour: Model as Muse, with Giselle Acosta ’27
description: Know Before You Go How to join: Check in at the Visitor Services desk; space is limited. Fee: This is a free event. Accessibility accommodations: If you would like to request accommodations for your visit, please contact Visitor Services at am_register@harvard.edu or 617-495-9400. For more details about accommodations at the museums, please see the Accessibility page.General info: The museum visit page has general guidelines for your visit. On this tour, Giselle Acosta ’27 will explore the lens through which artists depict their models, specifically the ones they elevate to the venerable rank of muse. The works on the tour will be Dante Gabriel Rossetti’s A Sea-Spell(1875–77), Ernst Ludwig Kirchner’s Self-Portrait with Cat (1920), and a 13-century Persian plaque. Spotlight Tours are designed and led by Harvard undergraduates from a range of academic disciplines. Each tour is focused on objects chosen by the student and provides visitors a unique, thematic view into the collections. Tours typically feature three works of art, embrace a conversational format, and last about 45 minutes. Open to the public, these tours start outside the museum shop on Saturdays and Sundays at 11am and 2pm. This program is supported by the Ho Family Student Guide Fund. The Ho Family Student Guide Program at the Harvard Art Museums prepares students to develop original, research-based tours. Through their training, Student Guides gain knowledge of the collections and develop skills in critical thinking, visual analysis, public speaking, and leadership. Find out what the Student Guides are up to anytime on Instagram @harvardarthappens.

description: This class is for people who wish to become better performers, runway artists and posing artists. This class is also for dancers who want to learn the techniques of Waacking. Their job is to sell the garment, and to exude absolute style on the runway. This class will help students through whatever they are going through in life with a walk. I believe that when we walk or move ahead, we conquer our fears just by moving forward. This class will help you learn how to flow with rhythm, pose with intention and twirl in grace. Waacking is a style that can be used on any runway, stage or platform. It’s rooted in Queer gay club culture and was fine tuned through underground disco music by gay men who had dance through exclusion and slurs. Waacking derived from Punking and has evolved into today’s dance culture all over the world. In this dance we will learn how to develop musicality, rhythmic arm patterns, and how to ooze out our emotions while creating visual art. This class will help students dance on cue, freestyle, and learn the rhythm of Waacking. But most of all, you will learn work the floor with this dance.
