Tap dancing began as an answer to the horrors of colonial enslavement…with no musical instruments, Irish and West African slaves turned to their own feet to create rhythms and percussion while pulling movement and technique from traditional tribal and cultural dances. Sounds were initially made with wooden soles, then pennies and bottle caps, finally becoming the modern metal plates screwed to the ball and heel of the shoes. These dances made their way to minstrel and vaudeville shows, eventually transforming into the broadway and rhythm style tap dancing we know today. Flamenco is a form of song, dance, and instrumental (mostly guitar) music commonly associated with the Andalusian Roma (Gypsies) of southern Spain. (There, the Roma people are called Gitanos.) The roots of flamenco, though somewhat mysterious, seem to lie in the Roma migration from Rajasthan (in northwest India) to Spain between the 9th and 14th centuries. These migrants brought with them musical instruments, such as tambourines, bells, and wooden castanets, and an extensive repertoire of songs and dances. In Spain they encountered the rich cultures of the Sephardic Jews and the Moors. Their centuries-long cultural intermingling produced the unique art form known as flamenco. (https://www.britannica.com/art/flamenco) What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I have been dancing and performing flamenco professionally for over 30 years. I have studied both here and in Spain, and continue my studies (to keep current with the dance) at various workshops both here and abroad. title: All About Lily Chou-Chou
description: Directed by Iwai Shunji, 2001. Adapted from a novel Iwai Shunji had developed through an online forum, All About Lily Chou-Chou follows a group of middle-school students whose lives are shaped by an increasingly digital world. The film’s fractured narrative is populated by anonymous internet message boards devoted to the fictional pop star Lily Chou-Chou as its young characters explore the depths and dangers of life online years before the ubiquity of social media. Confronting difficult subjects—violence, abuse, extreme alienation—it is equally a film about music, memory and the ways people seek beauty in the midst of suffering. "Ether," a transcendent quality that Lily's fans believe exists within her music, captures this ineffable, modern longing. With distinctive digital cinematography, evocative sound design and a hauntingly beautiful score by Kobayashi Takeshi, the film also remains strikingly contemporary more than twenty years after its release—anticipating many of the anxieties surrounding identity, technology and human connection that continue to define our present. – Max Surprenant ‘26 Part of the series Nostalgia, A Harvard Undergraduate Cinematheque Program. Capoeira Angola developed in Brazil from a variety of African roots. N’golo from Angola, rhythms from Congo, and acrobatics from Guinea combined to form a martial art disguised as a dance and played like a game. All these elements plus a deliberate sense of fun result in a vigorous workout for the body and mind! I saw Capoeira played on the streets, and was curious to know more. I fell in love with the music, history, and movements of the style. I graduated as a Mestre in 1984 and moved to Boston in 1986. I was the first to teach Capoeira in New England. Mestre Joao Pequenho certified me as a teacher of Capoeira Angola in 1991. Contra Mestre Calango: I moved to Boston in 2000 to continue training with Mestre Deraldo. Since then, I traveled with him to universities and events around the world to assist in demonstrating and teaching of the beautiful art of Capoeira Angola. I graduated as a Contra Mestre in 2017. title: The X-Tet Sounds of Italy
description: The X-tet returns with a sweeping celebration of Italian Baroque and Renaissance music , joined by GRAMMY® award-winning soprano Amanda Forsythe and viola da gamba player Cristiano Contadin . Spanning four centuries of Italy’s most treasured chamber repertoire, the ensemble brings to life virtuosic works by Vivaldi, Albinoni, Castello, and Handel alongside rarely heard gems by Maria Teresa Agnesi and Antonio Archilei. Highlights include Handel’s dramatic cantata “Armida abbandonata” and Archilei’s celestial “Dalle più alte sfere,” both featuring Forsythe’s celebrated voice, alongside instrumental showpieces for strings, theorbo, and harpsichord. The program concludes with a nod to folk tradition in the spirited Tarantella Gargano, before Colin Jacobsen’s new work , Morgantina Studies, brings the evening to a close. When their resistance turns deadly, Schroeder must grow up in the shadow of her father’s murder while Power disappears and spends decades on the FBI’s Most Wanted List. Years later, when Power resurfaces seeking redemption, she must confront Schroeder and the past that shaped their lives. Unfolding like a true crime thriller, this remarkable story asks: How far is too far in the fight to do what’s right?

title: Spotlight Tour: Coloring the Past, with Jide Anekwe ’28
description: Know Before You Go How to join: Check in at the Visitor Services desk; space is limited. Fee: This is a free event. Accessibility accommodations: If you would like to request accommodations for your visit, please contact Visitor Services at am_register@harvard.edu or 617-495-9400. For more details about accommodations at the museums, please see the Accessibility page.General info: The museum visit page has general guidelines for your visit. On this tour, Jide Anekwe ‘28 will look at the significance of color in the ancient Mediterranean world and at modern perceptions of the past. The stops on the tour are: Portrait of a woman, a painting from Roman Imperial Egypt (c. 130–150 CE); Youthful hero or god, a marble sculpture from Imperial Rome (1st–2nd century CE) after a Greek sculpture by Skopas from the fourth century BCE; and William Holman Hunt’s painting The Miracle of the Sacred Fire, Church of the Holy Sepulchre (1892–99). Spotlight Tours are designed and led by Harvard undergraduates from a range of academic disciplines. Each tour is focused on objects chosen by the student and provides visitors a unique, thematic view into the collections. Tours typically feature three works of art, embrace a conversational format, and last about 45 minutes. Open to the public, these tours start outside the museum shop on Saturdays and Sundays at 11am and 2pm. This program is supported by the Ho Family Student Guide Fund. The Ho Family Student Guide Program at the Harvard Art Museums prepares students to develop original, research-based tours. Through their training, Student Guides gain knowledge of the collections and develop skills in critical thinking, visual analysis, public speaking, and leadership. Find out what the Student Guides are up to anytime on Instagram @harvardarthappens.

About Música Criolla Born from the blend of Indigenous, African, and Spanish rhythms, melodies, and expressions, Peruvian música criolla gained widespread popularity in the early to mid-20th century. Its Golden Era during the 1940s and 1950s established many of the classic songs and dances enjoyed today, including the Peruvian vals, marinera, tondero, polca criolla, and Afro-Peruvian festejo and landó. description: Know Before You Go How to join: Check in at the Visitor Services desk; space is limited. Fee: This is a free event. Accessibility accommodations: If you would like to request accommodations for your visit, please contact Visitor Services at am_register@harvard.edu or 617-495-9400. For more details about accommodations at the museums, please see the Accessibility page.General info: The museum visit page has general guidelines for your visit. On this tour, Ricardo Fernandes Garcia ’27 will explore how representations of innocence have enabled artists to address conflict and war. The stops on the tour are Winslow Homer’s The Brush Harrow (1865), which depicts a scene from childhood; George Grosz’s Nutcracker(1931), which features a group of toys; and Joseph Cornell’s Midnight Carrousel (1954), which suggests the imagination at work. Spotlight Tours are designed and led by Harvard undergraduates from a range of academic disciplines. Each tour is focused on objects chosen by the student and provides visitors a unique, thematic view into the collections. Tours typically feature three works of art, embrace a conversational format, and last about 45 minutes. Open to the public, these tours start outside the museum shop on Saturdays and Sundays at 11am and 2pm. This program is supported by the Ho Family Student Guide Fund. The Ho Family Student Guide Program at the Harvard Art Museums prepares students to develop original, research-based tours. Through their training, Student Guides gain knowledge of the collections and develop skills in critical thinking, visual analysis, public speaking, and leadership. Find out what the Student Guides are up to anytime on Instagram @harvardarthappens.

title: Tom Swafford Quartet / John McDonald
description: $15 admission / 3pm doors / 3:30 show / seated / all ages Composer/violinist Tom Swafford presents a set of his solo piano compositions performed by John McDonald. The second set will feature Tom, violin, Brian Price, clarinet and saxophone, Nate McBride, bass, and Curt Newton, drums, performing improvisations based on selected themes and motives from those pieces. The concert will include a set of piano variations on Joann’s Green Satin Dress by Butch Morris, which the improvisors will interpret as well. Tom played in series of a large ensemble performances led by the esteemed conductor and composer Butch Morris in the fall of 2011. In that series, Morris incorporated his notated works into his practice of Conduction™ (conducted improvisation). This is an inspiration for today’s concert. John McDonald recently retired after 36 years as composition professor at Tufts University. John was a great inspiration for Tom, who studied with him at Tufts from 1991-1995. In addition to composition instruction, John co-led the NME (New Music Ensemble), which was Tom’s first exposure to free improvisation. Tom has been involved in free improv along with his fully notated composition work since that time. Prior to Tufts, Tom studied jazz piano and played in his high school jazz ensemble in Seattle. The jazz tradition continues to be an important factor in his compositional approach. Another fun fact is that Tom and Nate McBride played in the band in a Seattle Children’s Theatre production in the late 1980s, when Tom was in 8th grade and Nate was in high school! Tom is excited to once again collaborate with John, Nate, and this group of excellent Boston area improvisors.

title: Marie Antoinette
description: Directed by Sofia Coppola, 2006. A fourteen-year-old girl leaves her home, her country and her puppy behind to marry a man she has never met. Twenty years later, she is the most despised woman in France. Sofia Coppola’s Marie Antoinette explores the rigid social structure and wild excesses of Versailles on the eve of the French Revolution. The film’s setting, shot on location, is extravagant, immense and overwhelming. The characters often seem to be swallowed up by the very architecture and landscape over which they rule. Casting actors known for comedy—Steve Coogan, Rose Byrne, Jason Schwartzman—highlights the understated humor running through a film that is fully aware of aristocratic absurdity without ever quite making it a punchline. Part of the series Marie Antoinette and Friends, Three Films by Sofia Coppola. Screening on film.

title: Harvard Square French Fry & Pairings Food Tour
description: Harvard Square is famous for so much — Harvard University, eclectic bookshops, buskers, and a food scene that punches well above its weight. But here’s what most visitors don’t know: it’s also home to some of the best french fries in all of Massachusetts . Together with our guide Larom, a Harvard alum, we built an entire tour around that fact, and it’s become one of the most unique food experiences in Cambridge. On this 90-minute walking adventure, you’ll sample distinctly different styles of fries at three beloved Harvard Square spots — from classic hand-cut wedges to smoky BBQ fries to legendary sweet potato fries — each paired with a drink chosen specifically to bring out the flavors. We’ll try the original raspberry lime rickey , a refreshing peach lemonade , and a crazy ice cream frappe that has to be seen to be believed. All pairings are non-alcoholic, making this tour genuinely fun for the whole family. Along the way, your guide will walk you through the beloved cobblestone streets past Harvard Yard , the Widener Library , the quirky Harvard Lampoon building , and the storied Harvard Faculty Club — sharing the funny, fresh, and occasionally absurd stories that make this neighborhood unlike anywhere else in Boston. You’ll also hear the full saga of the French Fry Wars of the late 20th Century , a deliciously bizarre chapter of local food history that explains why Harvard Square’s fry scene is what it is today. This food tour is ideal for: Visitors to Boston looking for a memorable, off-the-beaten-path Cambridge experience Families with kids and teens who want something interactive and delicious Date nights — quirky, fun, and plenty of good food Birthday celebrations and small group outings Local students, grad students, alums, and neighbors who want to see a new side of Harvard!

description: $15 admission / Start 8:30pm / Doors 8pm / Seated Show Modern jazz played by Boston's best jazz musicians. Joe Hunt is a jazz drummer, educator, author, and historian. In the early 1960s, Joe Hunt performed and recorded alongside the late NEC Distinguished Artist-in-Residence Emeritus George Russell, with releases on Decca and Riverside. Hunt joined The Stan Getz Quartet in 1964, recording several releases on Verve, then was a member of the Bill Evans Trio from 1966-1967. The remainder of the 1960s found Hunt performing or recording with several other jazz luminaries including Chet Baker, Eric Dolphy, Dizzy Gillespie, Dexter Gordon, Charles Mingus, Bob Brookmeyer, and the late Herb Pomeroy. In the 1970s and 1980s, Hunt was a member of The National Jazz Ensemble, led jazz groups with John Scofield, Mike Stern, and Santi Debriano, and toured with quartets of Red Rodney and Hal McKusick. The 1990s, and beyond, have included membership in The Smithsonian Jazz Masters Orchestra, with former NEC president Gunther Schuller, performances with Kenny Burrell, Joe Lavano, Joanne Brackeen, and Tal Farlow, as well as recordings with the Bert Seager Quintet, and also, Trio. Hunt is the author of the 1994 book 52nd Street Beat, which is a historical look at jazz drummer greats from 1945 to 1965. The Joe Hunt quartet features a modern jazz ensemble music played by top local pros: Mark Pinto - alto saxophone, formerly years with the Buddy Rich band John Lockwood – bass, formerly with Joe Henderson, Lee Konitz, current Fringe member Yuka Hamano Hunt – piano, voice, arranger Joe Hunt – drums, formerly with George Russell, Stan Getz, Jim Hall, Dexter Gordon, and Bill Evans We pay tribute to a special composer or performer at most performances. Recent shows have included: Burt Bacharach, Ahmad Jamal, Bill Evans, and Gigi Gryce. description: The Dresselhaus Lecture series is named in honor of Mildred "Millie" Dresselhaus, a beloved MIT professor whose research helped unlock the mysteries of carbon, the most fundamental of organic elements—earning her the nickname “queen of carbon science.” This annual event recognizes a significant figure in science and engineering from anywhere in the world whose leadership and impact echo Millie’s life, accomplishments, and values. The 2026 Mildred S. Dresselhaus Lecture will be delivered by: Gang Chen Carl Richard Soderberg Professor of Power Engineering, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) Gang Chen is the Carl Richard Soderberg Professor of Power Engineering at Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). He served as the Department Head of the Department of Mechanical Engineering at MIT from 2013 to 2018. He obtained his PhD degree from the Mechanical Engineering Department at UC Berkeley under the supervision of then UC Berkeley Chancellor Chang-Lin Tien. He was a faculty member at Duke University and UCLA, before joining MIT in 2001. Chen's research spans from electrons and phonons transport in solid-state materials for thermoelectric energy conversion and microelectronic thermal management to evaporation and condensation for desalination and data center cooling. He received an NSF Young Investigator Award, an R&D 100 award, an ASME Heat Transfer Memorial Award, an ASME Frank Kreith Award in Energy, a Nukiyama Memorial Award by the Japan Heat Transfer Society, a World Technology Network Award in Energy, an Eringen medal from the Society of Engineering Science, the Capers and Marion McDonald Award for Excellences in Mentoring and Advising from MIT, a Steven Chu medal from the Asian American Academy of Science and Engineering, and an American Courage Award from Asian American Advancing Justice. title: History of Now Lectures Series - A Different Critique: MENA Jewish Approaches to Zionism and Imperialism, 1830-1948
description: History at MIT invites you to join us on Thursday, November 19th at 5 pm in E51-095 for the final lecture in the History of Now series, featuring Orit Bashkin, the Mabel Greene Myers Professor of Modern Middle Eastern History and Director of Graduate Studies, Modern Fields at the University of Chicago. Her talk is titled "A Different Critique: MENA Jewish Approaches to Zionism and Imperialism, 1830-1948." Orit Bashkin Mabel Greene Myers Professor of Modern Middle Eastern History Director of Graduate Studies, Modern Fields University of Chicago Thursday, November 19, 2026 5-6:30 pm MIT Building E51, Room 095 About Orit Bashkin Orit Bashkin is a historian who works on the intellectual, social, and cultural history of the modern Middle East. She got her Ph.D. from Princeton University (2004), writing a thesis on Iraqi intellectual history under the supervision of Professors Robert Tignor and Samah Selim, and her BA (1995) and MA (1999) from Tel Aviv University. Since her graduation, she has been working as a professor of modern Middle Eastern history in the Department of Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations at the University of Chicago. Her publications deal with Iraqi history, the history of Iraqi Jews, the Arab cultural revival movement (the nahda) in the late 19th century, and the connections between modern Arab history and Arabic literature. Her current research project explores the lives of Iraqi Jews in Israel. To Attend All of these lectures are free and open to the public. More information on the lecture series is available here. For questions, please contact Professor Lerna Ekmekcioglu, Head of History at MIT, at lerna@mit.edu. We hope to see you there!

These dances made their way to minstrel and vaudeville shows, eventually transforming into the broadway and rhythm style tap dancing we know today. description: The Bowery Presents Liana Flores Get Your Tickets! Doors open at 7:00 PM Show begins at 8:00 PM Liana Flores Biog “This record is the story of the country girl moving to the city,” Liana Flores says. “It’s bossa nova meets pop, inspired by the people, relationships and glamour of city life.” Since the release of her acclaimed 2024 debut album Flower of the soul, British-Brazilian singer-songwriter Liana Flores has been at the forefront of a bossa nova revival. Drawing on the ‘60s sound of genre pioneers like Joao Gilberto alongside pop songwriting, Flores combines the dual aspects of her cultural heritage to create an emotive sound. Following extensive tour dates across North America, Asia and Europe, Flores now returns with a new EP, And so it goes…, that expands her palette to encompass the playful and ebullient experiences of moving from her rural hometown in Norfolk to St. Andrews before coming to London. The result is a six track collection that shifts between finger-picked guitar and gossamer bossa vocals of “So it goes” to the upbeat funk inflections of the heavy-grooving love song “So mysterious”, the Carole King-influenced folk storytelling of “Here to stay,” and the sprightly, glittering pop melodies of “Silvershoes.” “These songs were informed by my experiences living in the city and touring for the first time. I grew up and studied in small towns with nature in my surroundings, so that’s what came naturally in terms of lyrics. With So it goes, the lyrics are more centred on human connection, and I wanted to explore a part of my identity that’s more playful and matter-of-fact. I also wanted to challenge myself to write songs with strong melodies that would be fun to sing or to get ready to.” Raised by an immigrant Brazilian mother and British father in East Anglia, Flores first began learning music while listening to ‘80s and ‘90s bossa nova artists like Bebel Gilberto and Leila Pinheiro alongside Top 40 pop radio. title: Jerry Bergonzi Quartet
description: $15 @ the door / $10 students / 8:30 start / 8pm doors / seated Jerry Bergonzi , Tenor Saxophone Luther Gray , Drums Plamen Karadonev, Piano Sean Farias, Bass Special Guest , Trumpet A fine, high-powered tenor saxophonist with a tone influenced by John Coltrane, a mastery of chord changes, and a strong musical imagination, Jerry Bergonzi has long had an underground following in the Boston area. He started on clarinet when he was eight, switching to alto at 12, and finally to tenor two years later. Bergonzi was inspired early on by Sonny Rollins, Coltrane, and Hank Mobley. He attended Lowell University and then after graduation played electric bass in local bands behind singers and strippers, saving up enough money to move to New York in 1972. After struggling in the Big Apple for seven years and gaining some recognition as a member of Two Generations of Brubeck and of the Dave Brubeck Quartet (with whom he appeared on several Concord albums during 1979-1981), Bergonzi moved back to Boston in 1981, where he developed a strong career both as a tenorman and as an educator. He has since led several groups (including two called Con Brio and Gonz) and recorded for the Plug, Not Fat, Red, and Blue Note labels. — By Scott Yanow, AllMusic Continuing Every Monday at 8:30pm Lineup subject to change

title: Online Seminar On Undergraduate Mathematics Education
description: Speaker: Alice Mark (Vanderbilt University) Title: Reframing “buy-in” during a phased adoption of course coordination Abstract: One of the major sticking points for departments thinking of coordinating their courses is buy-in from faculty. Will coordination mean that certain people just don’t teach that course? Do people just have to get on board, like it or not? Who has a say, and how? Do some faculty just get to opt out of the whole endeavor? Perhaps most importantly, how do we remain in collegial dialogue when we’ve decided to do this but don’t agree on all aspects of implementation? This session will not answer these questions. Rather, it will provide the opportunity to unpack them and brainstorm strategies relevant to your own course coordination project. title: Natasha Boutureira Exhibit Reception
description: Join us at the Opening Reception for the new art exhibition by Natasha Boutureira. Natasha Boutureira is a Caracas born, Miami raised visual artist, whose work represents her experience as living between cultures. Artist Statement: My paintings explore the space I exist in as a Venezuelan immigrant, a third borderland shaped by overlapping cultures, memories, and experiences. I paint objects my family brought from Venezuela, using photographs of my parents’ apartment that feel familiar yet foreign, inherited rather than remembered. Through digital manipulation, CMYK color, distortion, and language drawn from my upbringing as a Venezuelan in Miami, I merge secondhand memories with lived experience. My work becomes a way of actively constructing the memories I cannot directly recall, exploring belonging as something constantly being made. @Bouuhaus

description: Attend one of our most beloved, longest standing brewery traditions: Trivia Tuesday! Every Tuesday swing by our Broadway taproom for our weekly trivia night. It’s free to compete, and winners get beer money. Here’s how it works: show up with your team of 2 – 6 players starting at 7:00 pm, when we’ll open the doors to the back taproom. Head down the hallway to the back, then snag a seat. All seating is first come first serve, so we recommend arriving early – there generally is a line! Questions rotate every week, and cover categories ranging from history, politics, sports, movies, pop culture, music, and more. We’d love to see you at either or both! Hungry? Munch on our signature giant soft pretzels or some crunchy nachos, which are available Tuesday evenings only. You’re also always welcome to bring your own food or order in, ask our staff for their favorite local recommendations. See you at trivia night! You must be 21+ attend, all guests will be asked to show valid government ID. Questions? Get in touch! You can reach us at events@lamplighterbrewing.com

She gained widespread recognition for composing the original soundtrack for the hit Netflix series Sex Education. Sweet Petunia Mairead Guy (they/them) and Maddy Simpson (she/her) met at Berklee College of Music in 2018, bonding over a shared love of Simon & Garfunkel and Gillian Welch & Dave Rawlings during a rehearsal delay. The album explores breakups, outgrown friendships, and self-discovery, with a title that nods to Flatt & Scruggs’ classic bluegrass tune. It blends the traditional folk that shaped the duo with the punk and DIY influences of their local scene. title: Intermediate/Advanced Ballet with Dean Vollick
description: Class begins with a thorough set of exercises at the barre that last from 30 to 45 minutes. Centre practice follows, and may consist of a battement tendu exercise, a battement jeté exercise, a grand battement exercise, small and/or large adage, stationary turns, traveling turns, and petite and grand allegro enchaînement (small and big jumps). Classes are structured so that the dancer warms up their feet, legs, hips and upper body gradually. As class progresses there are more changes of weight and eventually, sudden changes of direction. Please register in studio with the class assistant Accepted Payments: Cash, Check, Venmo What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Ballet originated in the Italian Renaissance courts around 1500 as large balls or spectacles that were performed by members of the royal court. The French king, Louis XIV, created the first academy and the positions, steps, and movements of the ballet were collected and codified. The spectacles began to be performed by artists that were trained in the academy, originally as part of an opera, and later as ballets that told a story through music, mime, and dance. Over the centuries ballet has influenced folk dance styles of many (mainly European) nations and, more recently, has been influenced by folk, modern, and contemporary forms of dance from all countries. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I had a professional dance career that spanned more than twenty years and included company work in both ballet and contemporary companies as well as dancing, choreographing, and teaching as a freelance artist.

title: Richard P. Stanley Seminar in Combinatorics
description: Speaker: Jim Propp (UMass Lowell and Radcliffe Institute) Title: Snake graphs and q-deformed real numbers Abstract: I'll present a statistical-mechanical construction of q-deformed real numbers, inspired by the q-deformed rational numbers [x]_q of Morier-Genoud and Ovsienko. The new construction admits two equivalent formulations: one in terms of random filters in snake posets and the other in terms of random dimer covers of snake graphs. I'll begin with a combinatorial approach to Stern's diatomic series and the Calkin–Wilf bijection via finite snake graphs, and then construct q-deformed rational numbers by introducing an activity parameter q into the model. For irrational values of x, the construction requires passing from finite to infinite snake graphs; the main technical step is to show that the associated limiting probability measures are well defined. The resulting q-deformation satisfies [[x]]_1 = x for all x>0. There's evidence that, wherever both [x]_q and [[x]]_q are defined, [[x]]_q = q [x]_q. For more details, see arXiv:2607.14332.

title: MIT Music Tech Speaker Series Presents: Mark Ethier
description: Tools for Musicians in the Age of AI: From iZotope to Berklee Music and technology have always co-evolved. Long before the synthesizer, innovations ranging from new tuning systems to the piano's sustain pedal haven’t just made music easier to produce — they’ve fundamentally changed what kind of music is possible to make. How will AI as an underlying technology fit into this history? Since I was an undergraduate at MIT, I’ve spent my career building tools for musicians and watching this interplay firsthand. Sometimes, new technology inspires the music itself, like how rhythmic delay helped inspire U2’s “Where the Streets Have No Name.” Other times, musicians drive the technology. At iZotope, our collaboration with BT on Stutter Edit took intricate audio effects that could require hours of studio editing and made them playable in real time onstage. I’ve also witnessed the impact of the democratization of music making. We helped build a path for musicians to launch careers from their bedrooms, but we also watched large-format studios close their doors. It’s too early to fully grasp how generative AI will impact creative possibilities and livelihoods, but I'll share some early signals from recent market research, including Berklee’s June 2026 report, In Sync: Music and Video 2026. Now, we’re entering a new phase: the democratization of tool building. With a quiet revolution of musicians vibe-coding their own tools, this story is far from over. In these moments of change, it’s often clear what is being lost. But we also have to wonder what new artistic expression becomes possible, and with the evolution of generative AI, question who gets to shape that change and benefit from it. title: Author Talk: A Pox on Fools
description: Join us for an engaging evening with author Thomas Levenson as he discusses his new book, "A Pox on Fools: The True Believers, Grifters, and Cynics Who Convinced Us to Reject Vaccines," in conversation with MIT Museum Director Michael John Gorman. Since the advent of smallpox inoculation in the eighteenth century, the idea that a disease introduced to the body in some lesser, weakened form might prevent full-blown infection has been one of the greatest public health insights of the modern era, inspiring the invention of numerous vaccines and saving countless human lives. But, just as humanity acquired the superhuman ability to stop infectious disease in its tracks, some feared we had gone too far, leading to skepticism that has hijacked public health discourse today. In three sweeping essays written for our current moment of scientific mistrust, Thomas Levenson searches for the origins of the most common arguments against vaccines: that they are unnatural; that they are more dangerous than the illnesses they claim to prevent; and that they are an affront to freedom. Each arose from the earliest development of particular vaccines and the campaigns to distribute them. Even as the pattern repeats, Levenson reveals how innocent that skepticism initially was and, in each case, how very human fears and questions ultimately turned into something darker, where no truth would be enough to overcome the doubt. Copies of A Pox on Fools will be available for purchase and signing after the talk, courtesy of the MIT Press Bookstore. A limited number of free tickets are available for full-time students with ID. Please reach out to museumregadmin@mit.edu.

title: The Festivals of Drunkenness in the Temple of Mut
description: Register for In-Person Register for Online The Temple of Mut is an ancient Egyptian sanctuary dedicated to the mother goddess Mut. From the early New Kingdom (c. 15th century BCE) through the Roman era, this temple was the setting for several festivals of drunkenness. The archaeological remains of a columned hall at Mut’s temple indicate that these celebrations took place during the reign of Queen Hatshepsut (c. 1479–1459 BCE). These included the annual Drunkenness Festival and the major Theban ritual known as the Beautiful Feast of the Valley. In this lecture, Betsy Bryan examines how these festivals were celebrated at Mut and at other sites in ancient Egypt, highlighting their participants, rituals, and religious purposes. Advance registration is recommended. Free event parking is available with registration. Parking will be available starting at 5pm. Register by November 17 to receive parking registration instructions. About the Speaker Betsy M. Bryan is a historian and art historian of ancient Egypt and is a specialist in the New Kingdom (ca. 1600–1100 BCE). As professor emerita of Egyptian art and archaeology at Johns Hopkins University, she teaches in the Department of Near Eastern Studies. Her research interests include the organization and production of art and its social and cultural meanings, including performance and expressions of ritual. Bryan’s studies on the cult of Mut-Sekhmet are cited often. Her long-term field projects in the Temple of Mut in South Karnak (2001–2025) and in the Theban Tomb 92 of the Royal Butler Suemniut (1993–2001) on the West Bank of Luxor have extended her research into the Second Intermediate Period, c. 1700–1550 BCE. Bryan has curated art exhibitions for the Cleveland Museum of Art and the National Gallery of Art and has been both Curator and Director of the Johns Hopkins Archaeological Museum throughout her career at Johns Hopkins University.

Linear Salsa is a hybrid dance that comes from Mambo (a Cuban style that was popularized in the 1950’s NYC Palladium). NY Mambo is a marriage of footwork and partner-work from Cuba (Aftro-Cuban movements, Cuban Son) and the U.S. (Jazz, Swing). Salsa is a marketing term popularized in the 1970’s to commodify all Latin music and dance to a U.S. audience. Circular Salsa primarily comes from the Cuban dance Casino, which itself originates from Cuban Son. Salsa is by nature transformational, multinational, and multigenerational, embodying the shared heritage of Latin music. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I was the assistant teacher of this class for over 2 years under Ricardo Contreras. I’ve been taking classes from Juan Lopez for over 7 years. I started my Salsa journey learning New York Style Salsa On2 in Worcester. I also work at the Havana Club

title: Live Blues & Roots Music Returns to Harvard Square: Wednesday Nights @ The Sea Hag Restaurant & Bar
description: The Sea Hag Restaurant & Bar and The Barrett Anderson Band are excited to announce a new weekly series, Blues & Roots Wednesdays , bringing live music back home to historic Harvard Square. “Cambridge, our fair city, and I share deep roots, and I’m thrilled to find a new musical home at The Sea Hag,” says Massachusetts-based singer/guitarist, Barrett Anderson. “Good music and good food are two of our most basic, fundamental needs,” he continues, “What great joy they give us. I am so happy to revel in that every Wednesday night with my dearest musical friends, and Kari and her incredible team at The Sea Hag. We go way back together, and I can’t imagine all the fun we have ahead.” Indeed, Anderson has strong connections to this scene. He remembers: “My first professional experience came when I was 15, backing up Muddy Waters’ band alums Pinetop Perkins and Bob Margolin at the original House of Blues on Winthrop Street. A few months after that I began busking, you’d often find me in Brattle Square or by the pit. This would have been mid/late 90s.” While still a teen, Anderson was a member of The Monster Mike Welch Band and Ronnie Earl & The Broadcasters (“Ronnie was my guitar hero. Then he was my teacher, then my boss. Now he’s my musical Father,” Anderson says), before eventually starting The Barrett Anderson Band in 2007. Anderson won a Boston Music Award (2013 Blues Artist of the Year), was on the Billboard charts (2020’s live album Hynoboogie spent 3 weeks on the Billboard Blues Album chart, peaking at #6), and was nominated for a Blues Music Award (2023 Band of the Year with Anthony Geraci & The Boston Blues All-Stars), all the while playing nationally, internationally, and locally in Cambridge and the greater Boston area. In addition to the musical roots, long-time locals may recognize Anderson from a decade serving tables and bartending at The Sea Hag’s sister establishment, Grendel’s Den, or from Abodeon, the mid-century modern shop started by his family. title: History of Now Lectures Series - A Different Critique: MENA Jewish Approaches to Zionism and Imperialism, 1830-1948
description: History at MIT invites you to join us on Thursday, November 19th at 5 pm in E51-095 for the final lecture in the History of Now series, featuring Orit Bashkin, the Mabel Greene Myers Professor of Modern Middle Eastern History and Director of Graduate Studies, Modern Fields at the University of Chicago. Her talk is titled "A Different Critique: MENA Jewish Approaches to Zionism and Imperialism, 1830-1948." Orit Bashkin Mabel Greene Myers Professor of Modern Middle Eastern History Director of Graduate Studies, Modern Fields University of Chicago Thursday, November 19, 2026 5-6:30 pm MIT Building E51, Room 095 About Orit Bashkin Orit Bashkin is a historian who works on the intellectual, social, and cultural history of the modern Middle East. She got her Ph.D. from Princeton University (2004), writing a thesis on Iraqi intellectual history under the supervision of Professors Robert Tignor and Samah Selim, and her BA (1995) and MA (1999) from Tel Aviv University. Since her graduation, she has been working as a professor of modern Middle Eastern history in the Department of Near Eastern Languages and Civilizations at the University of Chicago. Her publications deal with Iraqi history, the history of Iraqi Jews, the Arab cultural revival movement (the nahda) in the late 19th century, and the connections between modern Arab history and Arabic literature. Her current research project explores the lives of Iraqi Jews in Israel. To Attend All of these lectures are free and open to the public. More information on the lecture series is available here. For questions, please contact Professor Lerna Ekmekcioglu, Head of History at MIT, at lerna@mit.edu. We hope to see you there!

title: Harvard Square French Fry & Pairings Food Tour
description: Harvard Square is famous for so much — Harvard University, eclectic bookshops, buskers, and a food scene that punches well above its weight. But here’s what most visitors don’t know: it’s also home to some of the best french fries in all of Massachusetts . Together with our guide Larom, a Harvard alum, we built an entire tour around that fact, and it’s become one of the most unique food experiences in Cambridge. On this 90-minute walking adventure, you’ll sample distinctly different styles of fries at three beloved Harvard Square spots — from classic hand-cut wedges to smoky BBQ fries to legendary sweet potato fries — each paired with a drink chosen specifically to bring out the flavors. We’ll try the original raspberry lime rickey , a refreshing peach lemonade , and a crazy ice cream frappe that has to be seen to be believed. All pairings are non-alcoholic, making this tour genuinely fun for the whole family. Along the way, your guide will walk you through the beloved cobblestone streets past Harvard Yard , the Widener Library , the quirky Harvard Lampoon building , and the storied Harvard Faculty Club — sharing the funny, fresh, and occasionally absurd stories that make this neighborhood unlike anywhere else in Boston. You’ll also hear the full saga of the French Fry Wars of the late 20th Century , a deliciously bizarre chapter of local food history that explains why Harvard Square’s fry scene is what it is today. This food tour is ideal for: Visitors to Boston looking for a memorable, off-the-beaten-path Cambridge experience Families with kids and teens who want something interactive and delicious Date nights — quirky, fun, and plenty of good food Birthday celebrations and small group outings Local students, grad students, alums, and neighbors who want to see a new side of Harvard!

title: Co-Adaptive—Ruth Mandl and Bobby Johnston
description: Co-Adaptive—Ruth Mandl and Bobby Johnston Part of the MIT Fall 2026 Architecture Lecture Series Presented with the Architecture and Urbanism Group CO₂ COAdaptive As our planet gets hotter, and more extreme weather events become the norm, CO Adaptive is positioning themselves as an unbuild, design and build practice: a new model that reunites designers and builders through collaboration in order to re-think our joint role in shaping the built environment; contending with architecture at the intersection of saving embodied carbon and reducing operational energy. As stewards of the existing material repository contained in our cities, CO Adaptive aims to increase the resilience and reusability of all that already surrounds us. Their talk will engage the breadth of the practice’s work—from adaptive reuse projects and high-efficiency retrofits to material salvage operations, remanufacturing, and design for disassembly. These projects yield a critical perspective on how buildings and materials re-engage in their next iteration of use, working towards a reality in which extractive and depleting habits are replaced by a circular library of abundance. CO Adaptive is an unbuild-design-build practice founded by Ruth Mandl and Bobby Johnston in 2011. Initially it was started as an architecture practice, focused on retrofitting existing building stock to create energy efficient, climate resilient and spatially beautiful environments. To have a greater impact on the process of taking old buildings apart—emphasizing deconstruction, and shaping attitudes about “waste”—CO Adaptive Building was established in 2021 and CO Adaptive Disassembly in 2026. The attention of all three intertwined practices is on converting existing buildings from a linear economy to a circular one. CO Adaptive’s work has received numerous awards and recognition, including winning the Architectural League’s Emerging Voices 2026, A|N’s 2025 Best of Practice Award, and the 2025 Trust for Governors Island Climat

title: The Life of George B. Schaller and the Future of Conservation
description: Advance registration is recommended. Register for In-Person Register for Online Speaker: Miriam Horn, Author Field biologist and conservationist George B. Schaller is renowned for revolutionizing the study of wildlife by observing animals in their natural habitats. He has also been a powerful advocate for protecting wilderness and animal species across the globe. Born in 1933 in Berlin to an American mother and a German father in Berlin, Schaller spent his war‑torn childhood searching for peace among wild creatures. His efforts took him around the world to study Congo mountain gorillas, Himalayan snow leopards, Brazilian jaguars, Tibetan brown bears, and many others. Before Jane Goodall or Dian Fossey, Schaller revealed the rich emotional and social lives of these primates and predators. Drawing from her new book Homesick for a World Unknown: The Life of George B. Schaller (Penguin Press, 2026), Miriam Horn will trace his remarkable career. She will highlight his views on conservation and the path to survival he mapped for us all—challenging us to rethink our place in the natural world. Copies of Homesick for a World Unknown will be available for purchase after the program. Free event parking is available with registration. Register by November 18 to receive parking registration instructions.

title: Materials Lab Workshop: Casting Connections—Molds, Replicas, and Questions of Authorship
description: Join research curator Francesca Bewer for a workshop focused on art and science. We’ll explore the intimate connections between models, molds, and casts; how molds and casts have been used to produce, replicate, and preserve three-dimensional objects; and what these objects can teach us about skill, technology, and value. Working with clay, plaster, wax, alginate, and silicone putty, we’ll experiment with different processes of molding and casting. Along the way, you’ll be introduced to the scientific tools used to investigate and identify the traces of process and change. Through discussion and comparison with historical plaster casts, wax models, and other surrogates in the Harvard Art Museums collections, we’ll ask when a copy might be considered “fake,” “genuine,” or something in between, and how replicas support research, teaching, and conservation in museums today. This workshop is one of four offered this fall that explore different media through the lens of art and science. Take one or take them all! The four workshops are: Saturday, September 19: Landscape Drawing with Optical DevicesWednesday, October 7: Color Alchemy—Pigments and DIY PaintFriday, November 6: Making an ImpressionFriday, November 20: Casting Connections—Molds, Replicas, and Questions of Authorship

title: Wang Lecture: Biophysics and Modeling Approaches for Development of Effective Downstream Bioprocesses of Complex Biological Products
description: Speaker: Steven M. Cramer, Institute Professor, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute Steve Cramer is an Institute Professor at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute. His laboratory develops models, materials, and processes to make downstream bioprocessing more effective for the purification of biological products. He is a member of the National Academy of Engineering, UT Austin’s Academy of Distinguished Chemical Engineers and an elected fellow of AAAS, AIChE, ACS and AIMBE. He has won numerous awards, including the Gordon Prize from the NAE, the ACS Separations Science and Technology Award, the BIOT Division’s Michael’s Award, the Gaden Award from Biotechnology and Bioengineering, the Wiley Distinguished Faculty Award and the School of Engineering Outstanding Professor and Research Excellence Awards from RPI. His inventions and models have been employed by numerous companies and he is active on industrial scientific advisory boards. The 65 PhD graduates from the Cramer lab have had a significant impact, with many former students now playing key leadership roles in the state of the art of industrial bioprocessing at major biopharmaceutical and bioseparations companies worldwide as well as in academia.

description: Boston Fiddle Funk Folk Festival at The Armory with Scottish Fish and Neil Pearlman & the Wallbreakers Boston based Scottish fiddle powerhouse Scottish Fish join forces with Neil Pearlman’s groundbreaking Celtic-Funk collective Neil Pearlman & the Wallbreakers for a high energy night of music with some of the country’s best Celtic, Funk and Jazz musicians under one roof! description: Classes teach Broadway style tap and focus on repetitive technique to encourage muscle memory and the confidence to create clear sounds. Inclusion is a priority so that all students feel welcome. Classes are “drop-in”, meaning you may join any week and there’s no “semester” commitment. Past steps are always reviewed with the introduction of 1 or 2 new steps or combos each class. Tap dancing began as an answer to the horrors of colonial enslavement…with no musical instruments, Irish and West African slaves turned to their own feet to create rhythms and percussion while pulling movement and technique from traditional tribal and cultural dances. Sounds were initially made with wooden soles, then pennies and bottle caps, finally becoming the modern metal plates screwed to the ball and heel of the shoes. These dances made their way to minstrel and vaudeville shows, eventually transforming into the broadway and rhythm style tap dancing we know today. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? Christina Harrington joined The Dance Complex as a Teaching Artist in May 2012. title: Flamenco Technique/Choreography Class with Sabrina Avilés
description: Classes will begin with a focus on technique, followed by choreography incorporating the mantón de Manila. Cost: $35 Single Class | $224 Entire Series (7 classes) REGISTER HERE What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Flamenco is a form of song, dance, and instrumental (mostly guitar) music commonly associated with the Andalusian Roma (Gypsies) of southern Spain. (There, the Roma people are called Gitanos.) The roots of flamenco, though somewhat mysterious, seem to lie in the Roma migration from Rajasthan (in northwest India) to Spain between the 9th and 14th centuries. These migrants brought with them musical instruments, such as tambourines, bells, and wooden castanets, and an extensive repertoire of songs and dances. In Spain they encountered the rich cultures of the Sephardic Jews and the Moors. Their centuries-long cultural intermingling produced the unique art form known as flamenco. (https://www.britannica.com/art/flamenco) What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I have been dancing and performing flamenco professionally for over 30 years. Throughout my career, I was also a member of three local flamenco companies: Ramon de los Reyes Spanish Dance Theatre, Omayra Amaya Flamenco Sin Limites and my own company, Flamenco Dance Project. I have studied both here and in Spain, and continue my studies (to keep current with the dance) at various workshops both here and abroad. Finish this statement: I am passionate about teaching this style because… it fills my soul, and I want to impart that to my students. I make it a point of really studying the different elements of the dance, especially el cante (singing) to teach my students the importance of the relationship between the dance and the singing. title: Soul Dance – An Embodied Movement Practice
description: A guided improvisational movement practice that engages somatic awareness to facilitate personal growth, emotional well-being, and collective healing. Welcoming participants of all experience levels, bodies and identities. We dance to expand and evolve our embodiment. We dance to release stored tension, emotions and patterns. We dance to integrate our experiences and we dance to remember who we really are. We enter in a cycle of movement that begins slow, builds in intensity, peaks, lightens, and then settles. Through verbal instructions, participants are invited to explore, in their own bodies way – a variety of movement patterns, physical inquiries, and focal points. The journey is curated to an intentional and eclectic world music soundscape. It is a journey where you might sweat (though you are always in control of your rhythm and pace).This class allows you to engage with the wisdom of your own body, to take you on a journey. This is a trauma-informed practice and container. GUIDELINES: Be on time PREPARATION: Wear clothing you can freely move and sweat in. Have water. title: Ashes and Diamonds
description: Directed by Andrzej Wajda, 1958. The last and loudest entry in Wajda’s WWII trilogy, Ashes and Diamonds adapts Jerzy Andrzejewski’s eponymous 1948 novel into one of Polish cinema’s strongest and most celebrated works. Set on May 8, 1945—Victory Day in Europe—after Red Army battalions had already expelled the occupier out of Poland, the historical thriller stars anti-Communist Home Army insurgents in a doomed underground plot to resist Soviet rule. In his performance as militant Maciek, Zbigniew Cybulski approaches and at times surpasses the youthful, tragic cool of James Dean, while Jerzy Wójcik’s stark camerawork ignites an inflammatory script into Wajda’s fiercest unraveling of national myth and taboo. Overflowing with Christian symbolism, the film was the director’s proudest achievement; it remains to this day a widely discussed touchstone of the Polish Film School and one of modern cinema’s richest interrogations of agency and belief in the face of futility and (overwhelming, ambivalent) defeat. Part of the series Once There Was History . Andrzej Wajda at 100.

title: Laurie MacAllister & Seth Glier at Club Passim
description: In late 2024, Laurie MacAllister embarked on an exciting new chapter, launching a solo career with a sold-out performance right here at legendary Club Passim. Two decades earlier, she co-founded the beloved Americana trio Red Molly, which released seven acclaimed albums and toured both the U.S. and internationally, including appearances at MerleFest, Cayamo, and Boston Symphony Hall. Along the way, ad executives heard Laurie’s voice on the Red Molly album “Never Been to Vegas” and invited her to sing the iconic Folgers Coffee jingle for a national TV commercial. Her 2018 self-produced solo album “The Lies the Poets Tell” is a heartfelt tribute to the contemporary folk music scene, celebrating a handful of its best songs and songwriters. It features duets with six male artists, including the late Americana master Jimmy LaFave. SiriusXM praised the album as “Defining. A curated collection packed with emotional vibrancy.” Laurie’s earlier solo album “The Things I Choose To Do” was produced by folk luminary Cliff Eberhardt and was first released independently. Hearing it, Barnes & Noble re-released it as an exclusive on their label, saying, “MacAllister wholly inhabits these songs as subtly as a chameleon, convincingly taking on the persona’s skin, quite simply singing her heart out.” From a young girl with a quiet dream of becoming a singer, Laurie’s journey has unfolded one song at a time. Over more than two decades, she’s made her dream into a reality.

title: A Generation
description: Directed by Andrzej Wajda, 1955. After witnessing Nazis slay his friend, young proletarian Stach joins a partisan resistance cell (the left-wing People’s Guard) and transforms as a person, lover and antifascist. Andrzej Wajda’s feature debut exudes energy and composure, shading 1942 Warsaw in Expressionist cinematography—courtesy of Jerzy Lipman—and a contrapuntal soundscape by the modernist composer Andrzej Markowski. Influences of Italian neorealism and urban documentary are apparent, as is Wajda’s ambition to devise a new Polish cinema on the ruins of the old and artificial. No actors with experience in prewar filmmaking were used; A Generation was the first professional project for most of the cast and crew. To appropriately imbue spaces with atmospheric dread, filming mostly took place on cloudy and rainy days, ensuring that Wajda’s first film is also among his darkest. Assistant director Kazimierz Kutz, meanwhile, provided one of film history’s earliest appearances of the “squib”—here, a condom filled with fake blood and dynamite, a technique used with explosive success to this day. Part of the series Once There Was History . Andrzej Wajda at 100.

title: Innocent Sorcerers
description: Directed by Andrzej Wajda, 1960. Wajda’s singular New Wave film—shot two months before À bout de souffle but released after—follows a noncommittal hipster through a series of pararomantic encounters in nightclubs, apartments and boxing rings. Dismissed both by early critics and the director (who subsequently called the early ’60s the “most difficult period” of his life), Innocent Sorcerers has since been reappraised as a key entry in postwar Polish cinema. Youth culture, jazz, motorbikes and promiscuity abound in a freshly-thawed Warsaw under the influence of Western capital and culture. History and politics are absent, with Wajda’s attention turned instead to the contemporary music scene he and then-twenty-year-old screenwriter Jerzy Skolimowski experienced at the Łódź Film School. Pianist Krzysztof Komeda composed the electrifying score and played himself in a cameo, where Zbigniew Cybulski also makes an appearance. One of Wajda’s liveliest films is also one of his best, soured only by a happy ending didactically tacked on at the eleventh hour by censors. Part of the series Once There Was History . Andrzej Wajda at 100.

title: Harvard Square French Fry & Pairings Food Tour
description: Harvard Square is famous for so much — Harvard University, eclectic bookshops, buskers, and a food scene that punches well above its weight. But here’s what most visitors don’t know: it’s also home to some of the best french fries in all of Massachusetts . Together with our guide Larom, a Harvard alum, we built an entire tour around that fact, and it’s become one of the most unique food experiences in Cambridge. On this 90-minute walking adventure, you’ll sample distinctly different styles of fries at three beloved Harvard Square spots — from classic hand-cut wedges to smoky BBQ fries to legendary sweet potato fries — each paired with a drink chosen specifically to bring out the flavors. We’ll try the original raspberry lime rickey , a refreshing peach lemonade , and a crazy ice cream frappe that has to be seen to be believed. All pairings are non-alcoholic, making this tour genuinely fun for the whole family. Along the way, your guide will walk you through the beloved cobblestone streets past Harvard Yard , the Widener Library , the quirky Harvard Lampoon building , and the storied Harvard Faculty Club — sharing the funny, fresh, and occasionally absurd stories that make this neighborhood unlike anywhere else in Boston. You’ll also hear the full saga of the French Fry Wars of the late 20th Century , a deliciously bizarre chapter of local food history that explains why Harvard Square’s fry scene is what it is today. This food tour is ideal for: Visitors to Boston looking for a memorable, off-the-beaten-path Cambridge experience Families with kids and teens who want something interactive and delicious Date nights — quirky, fun, and plenty of good food Birthday celebrations and small group outings Local students, grad students, alums, and neighbors who want to see a new side of Harvard!

title: Julia Minkin
description: Julia Minkin SHOW DESCRIPTION: Chicago-based singer-songwriter Julia Minkin is joined by Boston favorites Bowling Shoes and Cate Yoder for an evening of inventive indie music, compelling storytelling, and rich, genre-bending sounds. From shimmering synth-pop and art-rock experimentation to intimate folk melodies, this lineup offers music that’s as intelligent as it is fun. ARTIST BIOS: Julia Minken: Best known for co-writing viral hit songs with French electropop sensation Kid Francescoli, Chicago-based singer-songwriter Julia Minkin steps into her own with her debut album Not Ready, co-created and produced with her husband Andrew Sudhibhasilp. Blending warm, folk-tinged vocals with nostalgic dance-floor energy and introspection, Minkin “finds her own creative voice, shimmering, rhythmic, and heartfelt—both bold and refreshingly sincere” (Thoughts Words Actions). Bowling Shoes: Melding innovative art-pop experimentalism with indie-rock nuance and arena-ready hooks, Boston, MA’s Bowling Shoes craft eminently catchy music sprinkled with delightful touches of subversive noise Cate Yoder: A double and electric bassist and guitarist from Richmond, Virginia, Cate Yoder learns about her environment through exploring, inventing, and performing a multitude of genres or really any music she can get hands on. Since being established primarily as a bass player, she is diving into the songwriting indie folk role with her band of talented women, performing in the Boston area. With airy melodies, detailed guitar, piano, and percussive elements, and bitter lyrics, she hopes to share her experience of finding solace and comfort in a complex world. title: Carl M. Sapers Ethics in Practice Lecture: Sylvia Lavin “Architecture After Fire”
description: This lecture, “Architecture After Fire,” argues that the rise of American architectural modernism was inseparable from the forest, not because of the use of timber, but because of modernism’s reliance on arboreal media—employing trees as information and communication systems and as metaphors. Tracking the white pine through deforestation, wildfire, and the formation of the Chicago school, this paper explores the series of substitutions, each triggered by fire, that converted environmental catastrophe into aesthetic doctrine and designated these operations as the primary function of modern architecture, artistically considered.

title: Kanał
description: Directed by Andrzej Wajda, 1957. Gripping and tenebrous, Andrzej Wajda’s second feature resumes A Generation ’s interest in naturalist, anti-dogmatic tellings of wartime resistance, yet shifts focus to the underground Home Army, whose 1944 Warsaw Uprising was a pivotal (if ultimately doomed) attempt at liberation. The first film to tackle the tragic and contentious operation, Kanał descends into the capital’s sewers to observe the hopeless, Dantesque trek of exhausted platoons escaping the city in late September, when defeat was already inescapable. Jerzy Lipman returns as cinematographer, depicting the dank gutters—all built in the back lot of a Łódź studio—in an asphyxiating high-contrast palette. To make the film, Wajda benefitted from Gomułka’s Thaw which, however, did little to shield Kanał from harsh audience critique. “This film could not satisfy them,” Wajda later remarked. “They had licked their wounds, mourned their dead, and now they wanted to see their moral and spiritual victory, and not death in the sewers.” Unredemptive to its core, Wajda’s bleakest has since been rightfully recognized as one of world cinema’s great reckonings with impossible (yet necessary) roads to freedom. Part of the series Once There Was History . Andrzej Wajda at 100. Screening on film.

title: Boulez at 100
description: As part of the worldwide celebration of Pierre Boulez’s centenary, acclaimed pianists Gloria Cheng and Ralph van Raat bring their touring program Boulez at 100 to MIT, hosted by MIT Media Lab Faculty Director Tod Machover. The program interweaves Boulez’s seminal piano works with music by John Cage, Morton Feldman, Frank Zappa, Magnus Lindberg, and Olivier Messiaen–composers who each echo, anticipate, or challenge Boulez’s vision across modernist, experimental, and boundary-crossing traditions. Featuring chapters from Boulez’s rarely heard Structures Books I and II, the concert traces the rich artistic dialogue between Boulez and the composers whose music surrounds his own. Together, these works reveal Boulez not only as one of the twentieth century’s most influential composers, but also as an artist whose ideas have an increasing, surprising potential to resonate across generations, genres, and musical traditions.

He started on clarinet when he was eight, switching to alto at 12, and finally to tenor two years later. Bergonzi was inspired early on by Sonny Rollins, Coltrane, and Hank Mobley. He attended Lowell University and then after graduation played electric bass in local bands behind singers and strippers, saving up enough money to move to New York in 1972. After struggling in the Big Apple for seven years and gaining some recognition as a member of Two Generations of Brubeck and of the Dave Brubeck Quartet (with whom he appeared on several Concord albums during 1979-1981), Bergonzi moved back to Boston in 1981, where he developed a strong career both as a tenorman and as an educator. title: Voices Unheard
description: Voices Unheard SHOW DESCRIPTION: Voices Unheard: From the Margins to the Mic returns to Massachusetts for its seventh consecutive year, continuing its tradition of centering lived experience through story. The event features true narratives from adult storytellers who have submitted their work, sharing personal accounts of identity, origin, separation, and reunion. While participants come from a range of lived experiences—including adoption, foster care, donor conception, and unexpected family discoveries—the lineup reflects those who have chosen to step forward and share their stories this year. Together, these voices create a collective portrait of what it means to grow up without full access to one’s origins, and the ongoing search for connection, meaning, and belonging. ARTIST BIO: Lisa “LC” Coppola is a domestic DCF adoptee, writer, educator, and creator of the Voices Unheard Storytelling Program. She is the author of Voices Unheard: A Reflective Journal for Adult Adoptees and the essay Heartichoke, featured in the 2026 anthology Relative Strangers: Inheritance, Identity, and the Meaning of Kinship. Her debut novel, Monster Flower, is forthcoming from Jaded Ibis Press in Spring 2027. Kristal Parke is a talented filmmaker, producer, speaker and podcaster whose work explores identity, belonging, and resilience. A transracial adoptee from a closed adoption, her personal journey fuels her storytelling with authenticity, compassion, and truth. She creates space for unheard voices, shaping narratives that educate, challenge, inspire and heal. Anjali teaches in the unique style of Pandit Chitresh Das, founded in the Lucknow Gharana (style) with influence of the Jaipur Gharana along with a technique he developed called Kathak Yoga, where you will learn how we can integrate multiple rhythms through our dance. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? My kathak journey began with Gretchen Hayden, Founder of Chhandika Boston and Senior Disciple of Pandit Chitresh Das. Pandit Das was the pioneer of kathak dance bringing his rich training and upbringing in Kolkata, India to the US in 1971. I began my studies informally in 1997 while at Tufts University with Gretchenji and was hooked. From 2003 to 2011 I trained, taught, and toured as a member of the Chitresh Das Dance Company (CDDC) all across the US and India, holding lead roles such as Sita in Sita Haran. I have been steeped in this incredibly rich tradition of kathak, with it’s elements of dance, music, history, philosophy, math, and so much more and am thrilled to share with students and audiences widely in a manner that highlights how universal and accessible and FUN it really is! title: Intro to Balboa Fundamentals 1A & 1B
description: Fundamentals 1A assumes no dance experience at all, and will teach the fundamental connection techniques for partnered Balboa dancing, along with the primary figures of Balboa, and Fundamentals 1B refines those techniques and adds a few more figures. Class is taught ELEF (Everybody Leads Everybody Follows), which helps you better understand how both roles work and feel, so that beyond this series, you can choose the one that suits you, or choose to keep dancing in both! No partner is necessary, as we will rotate partners in class. PLEASE NOTE: CLASSES ARE CUMULATIVE, and drop-ins are not possible after the first 2 sessions of Fundamentals 1A. Balboa is a vernacular swing dance from Southern California in the 1920s and 30s, and is indebted to the African-American roots and culture of Swing Jazz and Swing dancing. We encourage everyone to explore the history of this dance, the dancers that created it in Southern California, and the music and musicians that made it possible. Balboa today is an improvisational, joyful partner dance with a vibrant worldwide community, evolving into the present while honoring its origins. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? July and Stan have danced Balboa since the early 2000s, learning from original SoCal dancers and the second-generation teachers who came after them. We both deeply love social partner-dancing, and we teach so that more people can participate in this joyful community of movement and connection. title: Red McAdam at Club Passim
description: On Comic Western Gothic, Red McAdam’s playful outsider country music shines; he presents an inventive vision of what the genre can be. A consummate road dog, he brings to this sophomore album the frenetic, dynamic, and occasionally delirious performances he spent years honing in dives, dancehalls, and theaters. In Red’s rich, risky blend of traditional honkytonk, folk and western swing, listeners will recognize the Lone Star eccentricities of Terry Allen and Guy Clark, forlorn folk sensibilities of Elizabeth Cotton and Karen Dalton, and the driving genre-bending of The Band and Little Feat.

title: Latina – Dance Fitness
description: No dance experience is needed to join this class! Classes are multi-level and combine easy-to-follow choreography with higher-energy movement, allowing students to learn the choreographies over time while moving at their own pace. My goal is to create a welcoming, judgment-free environment where students can get a great workout, build confidence, and most importantly, have fun dancing to music they love. Cost: $22 Single Class | $100 for 5 Classes | $180 for 10 Classes | $255 for 15 Classes *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. REGISTER HERE What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Latina Tribe is a dance fitness method primarily influenced by reggaeton and contemporary Latin music, while also incorporating elements of hip-hop, pop, and other dance styles. Reggaeton developed through a blend of Caribbean and Latin American influences, with roots in Panama and Puerto Rico and strong connections to reggae en español, dancehall, and hip-hop. Today, the genre has grown into a global cultural movement while remaining deeply connected to the Latin and Caribbean communities that shaped it. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I am a certified Senior Instructor with Latina Tribe, a dance fitness method focused on creating empowering spaces for women and members of the LGBTQ+ community. I began my journey with Latina Tribe as a student in 2021 and, after years of practicing the method, became a certified instructor and began teaching in 2024. Since then, I have continued my training and recently earned the Senior Instructor designation, which allows me to teach across all levels of the method. My main goal is to connect with every person that steps in my classes, creating a space where movement, fitness, community, and self-expression come together. Cost: $0 – $22 Sliding Scale REGISTER HERE What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Majestic Healing Pathways™ is the foundational care model that guides all of Majestic Community Wellness’s programs. It reflects our belief that healing is a right — not a privilege — and that healing happens most sustainably when care is consistent, culturally grounded, and rooted in community. Developed in response to gaps in traditional health and wellness systems, Majestic Healing Pathways™ centers the lived experiences of Black and Brown communities who face disproportionate stress, trauma, and barriers to care. The model honors the reality that healing is not a single intervention, but a pathway built over time through breath, movement, rest, relationship, and choice. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? For more than 20 years, Nora has been teaching yoga and dance to students of all ages. She completed her 200-hour teacher training at Atmananda Yoga, and her teaching continues to be informed by years of study in Pilates, Feldenkrais, Hot Yoga, and Katonah Yoga. The births of her two children inspired her to deepen her studies in prenatal and postnatal yoga. She focused much of her teaching on supporting families and children through the various stages of development. During this time, she earned her Prenatal Yoga Certification through OM Yoga

title: Intermediate/Advanced Ballet with Dean Vollick
description: Class begins with a thorough set of exercises at the barre that last from 30 to 45 minutes. Centre practice follows, and may consist of a battement tendu exercise, a battement jeté exercise, a grand battement exercise, small and/or large adage, stationary turns, traveling turns, and petite and grand allegro enchaînement (small and big jumps). Classes are structured so that the dancer warms up their feet, legs, hips and upper body gradually. As class progresses there are more changes of weight and eventually, sudden changes of direction. Live music is provided by a pianist, that ranges from classical pieces to selections from ballet repertoire to improvisational contemporary music. Cost: $20 Single Class | $15.00 barre | 5-class package $90.00 *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. Please register in studio with the class assistant Accepted Payments: Cash, Check, Venmo What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Ballet originated in the Italian Renaissance courts around 1500 as large balls or spectacles that were performed by members of the royal court. The French king, Louis XIV, created the first academy and the positions, steps, and movements of the ballet were collected and codified. The spectacles began to be performed by artists that were trained in the academy, originally as part of an opera, and later as ballets that told a story through music, mime, and dance. Over the centuries ballet has influenced folk dance styles of many (mainly European) nations and, more recently, has been influenced by folk, modern, and contemporary forms of dance from all countries. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I had a professional dance career that spanned more than twenty years and included company work in both ballet and contemporary companies as well as dancing, choreographing, and teaching as a freelance artist.

title: Live Blues & Roots Music Returns to Harvard Square: Wednesday Nights @ The Sea Hag Restaurant & Bar
description: The Sea Hag Restaurant & Bar and The Barrett Anderson Band are excited to announce a new weekly series, Blues & Roots Wednesdays , bringing live music back home to historic Harvard Square. “Cambridge, our fair city, and I share deep roots, and I’m thrilled to find a new musical home at The Sea Hag,” says Massachusetts-based singer/guitarist, Barrett Anderson. “Good music and good food are two of our most basic, fundamental needs,” he continues, “What great joy they give us. I am so happy to revel in that every Wednesday night with my dearest musical friends, and Kari and her incredible team at The Sea Hag. We go way back together, and I can’t imagine all the fun we have ahead.” Indeed, Anderson has strong connections to this scene. He remembers: “My first professional experience came when I was 15, backing up Muddy Waters’ band alums Pinetop Perkins and Bob Margolin at the original House of Blues on Winthrop Street. A few months after that I began busking, you’d often find me in Brattle Square or by the pit. This would have been mid/late 90s.” While still a teen, Anderson was a member of The Monster Mike Welch Band and Ronnie Earl & The Broadcasters (“Ronnie was my guitar hero. Then he was my teacher, then my boss. Now he’s my musical Father,” Anderson says), before eventually starting The Barrett Anderson Band in 2007. Anderson won a Boston Music Award (2013 Blues Artist of the Year), was on the Billboard charts (2020’s live album Hynoboogie spent 3 weeks on the Billboard Blues Album chart, peaking at #6), and was nominated for a Blues Music Award (2023 Band of the Year with Anthony Geraci & The Boston Blues All-Stars), all the while playing nationally, internationally, and locally in Cambridge and the greater Boston area. In addition to the musical roots, long-time locals may recognize Anderson from a decade serving tables and bartending at The Sea Hag’s sister establishment, Grendel’s Den, or from Abodeon, the mid-century modern shop started by his family. Linear Salsa is a hybrid dance that comes from Mambo (a Cuban style that was popularized in the 1950’s NYC Palladium). title: Harvard Square French Fry & Pairings Food Tour
description: Harvard Square is famous for so much — Harvard University, eclectic bookshops, buskers, and a food scene that punches well above its weight. But here’s what most visitors don’t know: it’s also home to some of the best french fries in all of Massachusetts . Together with our guide Larom, a Harvard alum, we built an entire tour around that fact, and it’s become one of the most unique food experiences in Cambridge. On this 90-minute walking adventure, you’ll sample distinctly different styles of fries at three beloved Harvard Square spots — from classic hand-cut wedges to smoky BBQ fries to legendary sweet potato fries — each paired with a drink chosen specifically to bring out the flavors. We’ll try the original raspberry lime rickey , a refreshing peach lemonade , and a crazy ice cream frappe that has to be seen to be believed. All pairings are non-alcoholic, making this tour genuinely fun for the whole family. Along the way, your guide will walk you through the beloved cobblestone streets past Harvard Yard , the Widener Library , the quirky Harvard Lampoon building , and the storied Harvard Faculty Club — sharing the funny, fresh, and occasionally absurd stories that make this neighborhood unlike anywhere else in Boston. You’ll also hear the full saga of the French Fry Wars of the late 20th Century , a deliciously bizarre chapter of local food history that explains why Harvard Square’s fry scene is what it is today. This food tour is ideal for: Visitors to Boston looking for a memorable, off-the-beaten-path Cambridge experience Families with kids and teens who want something interactive and delicious Date nights — quirky, fun, and plenty of good food Birthday celebrations and small group outings Local students, grad students, alums, and neighbors who want to see a new side of Harvard!

description: In this class, you’ll explore earthy Egyptian, Turkish, and American style movements, dynamic combinations, and expressive choreography blending tradition and innovation. The more authentic name for this dance form is raqs sharqi (“dance of the East”), and its roots lie in the Middle and Near East, primarily in Egypt and Turkey. This dance form was introduced to the United States and Europe at the turn of the 20th century, but it was not widely performed or taught until the 1950s and 1960s, when the belly dance craze swept across the U.S. The American cabaret style of belly dance is rooted in the legacy passed down by notable American teachers and performers, who blended Middle Eastern influences with their own innovations and movement styles drawn from diverse dance backgrounds. Tap is an American dance form in which rhythms are audibly tapped out on the floor. It has origins in slavery and the percussive dances of West African Juba dance and Irish step dancing.
