title: The Promised Land
description: Directed by Andrzej Wajda, 1975. “The Pope—now that’s a company!” One of the great films about capitalism, Wajda’s The Promised Land turns Nobel laureate Władysław Reymont’s 1899 novel into a three-hour epic of finance, opportunism and deception. In 1880s Łódź, three entrepreneurial men set out to ride the Industrial Revolution by opening a cotton processing plant, enriching (and irredeemably destroying) themselves in the process. Extreme wide-angle lensing—which Wajda had already employed to great effect in The Ashes —turns looms and mills into ominous objects, further made alien by Wojciech Kilar’s avant-garde score. Locations were effortless to source, as Łódź—Poland’s answer to Manchester—had kept early factory interiors intact, machines and offices included. In adapting Reymont, Wajda aimed to expunge the plot of ethnic stereotypes, traces of which nevertheless remain. So too does the director’s ambition to make what he called an “American” film, edited with zest, suspense and more than a little unabashed spectacle (as well as gore). Part of the series Once There Was History . Andrzej Wajda at 100.

Flamenco is a form of song, dance, and instrumental (mostly guitar) music commonly associated with the Andalusian Roma (Gypsies) of southern Spain. (There, the Roma people are called Gitanos.) The roots of flamenco, though somewhat mysterious, seem to lie in the Roma migration from Rajasthan (in northwest India) to Spain between the 9th and 14th centuries. These migrants brought with them musical instruments, such as tambourines, bells, and wooden castanets, and an extensive repertoire of songs and dances. In Spain they encountered the rich cultures of the Sephardic Jews and the Moors. Their centuries-long cultural intermingling produced the unique art form known as flamenco. title: Man of Marble
description: Directed by Andrzej Wajda, 1977. The best and fiercest of Wajda’s ’70s political films, Man of Marble was stuck in development inferno for over a decade. Authorities greenlit the production in 1976, spurring Aleksander Ścibor-Rylski to update the script according to changed (which is to say liberalized) conditions of his present. Student director Agnieszka—Krystyna Janda in the first of four Wajda appearances—sets out to investigate the life of Mateusz Birkut, a Stakhanovite shock force worker in 1950s Nowa Huta who has since unceremoniously vanished. Newsreels, reenactment and absurdist fiction join forces in a bravado of critical cinema that obsessed masses at home and elsewhere. One fifth of Poland caught the 1977 theatrical release, while Jean-Luc Godard raved about Janda’s “critical eyes of freedom” in Cahiers du Cinéma . An inspired disassembly of myth, propaganda and media manipulation, the film was also instrumental in prefiguring (and fomenting) trade union movements that would roil the country only three years later. Part of the series Once There Was History . Andrzej Wajda at 100.

title: Spotlight Tour: Child’s Play, with Ricardo Fernandes Garcia ’27
description: Know Before You Go How to join: Check in at the Visitor Services desk; space is limited. Fee: This is a free event. Accessibility accommodations: If you would like to request accommodations for your visit, please contact Visitor Services at am_register@harvard.edu or 617-495-9400. For more details about accommodations at the museums, please see the Accessibility page.General info: The museum visit page has general guidelines for your visit. On this tour, Ricardo Fernandes Garcia ’27 will explore how representations of innocence have enabled artists to address conflict and war. The stops on the tour are Winslow Homer’s The Brush Harrow (1865), which depicts a scene from childhood; George Grosz’s Nutcracker(1931), which features a group of toys; and Joseph Cornell’s Midnight Carrousel (1954), which suggests the imagination at work. Spotlight Tours are designed and led by Harvard undergraduates from a range of academic disciplines. Each tour is focused on objects chosen by the student and provides visitors a unique, thematic view into the collections. Tours typically feature three works of art, embrace a conversational format, and last about 45 minutes. Open to the public, these tours start outside the museum shop on Saturdays and Sundays at 11am and 2pm. This program is supported by the Ho Family Student Guide Fund. The Ho Family Student Guide Program at the Harvard Art Museums prepares students to develop original, research-based tours. Through their training, Student Guides gain knowledge of the collections and develop skills in critical thinking, visual analysis, public speaking, and leadership. Find out what the Student Guides are up to anytime on Instagram @harvardarthappens.

title: Wałęsa: Man of Hope
description: Directed by Andrzej Wajda, 2013. “This film is going to be the hardest of my career,” intimated Andrzej Wajda during preproduction on Wałęsa: Man of Hope . “I don’t want to, but I have to [make it],” the director quipped, using Lech Wałęsa’s own words about running for president in 1990. Almost two decades Wałęsa’s senior, Wajda was eighty-seven at the film’s premiere; he would go on to finish one last feature, the extraordinary Afterimage in 2016. A late addition to what the filmmaker called his Solidarity “triptych,” Wałęsa is an uncommonly propulsive biopic of the union leader, Nobel laureate and democratic statesman, who reportedly approved of Wajda’s portrayal. As in Man of Marble and Man of Iron , documentary and reportage are interlaced with fictional scenarios of Wałęsa (mostly) excelling in the public and private sphere. Robert Więckiewicz shines as the titular rebel, showing late Wajda in good control of cast, crew and national legend. Part of the series Once There Was History . Andrzej Wajda at 100.

title: Harvard Square French Fry & Pairings Food Tour
description: Harvard Square is famous for so much — Harvard University, eclectic bookshops, buskers, and a food scene that punches well above its weight. But here’s what most visitors don’t know: it’s also home to some of the best french fries in all of Massachusetts . Together with our guide Larom, a Harvard alum, we built an entire tour around that fact, and it’s become one of the most unique food experiences in Cambridge. On this 90-minute walking adventure, you’ll sample distinctly different styles of fries at three beloved Harvard Square spots — from classic hand-cut wedges to smoky BBQ fries to legendary sweet potato fries — each paired with a drink chosen specifically to bring out the flavors. We’ll try the original raspberry lime rickey , a refreshing peach lemonade , and a crazy ice cream frappe that has to be seen to be believed. All pairings are non-alcoholic, making this tour genuinely fun for the whole family. Along the way, your guide will walk you through the beloved cobblestone streets past Harvard Yard , the Widener Library , the quirky Harvard Lampoon building , and the storied Harvard Faculty Club — sharing the funny, fresh, and occasionally absurd stories that make this neighborhood unlike anywhere else in Boston. You’ll also hear the full saga of the French Fry Wars of the late 20th Century , a deliciously bizarre chapter of local food history that explains why Harvard Square’s fry scene is what it is today. This food tour is ideal for: Visitors to Boston looking for a memorable, off-the-beaten-path Cambridge experience Families with kids and teens who want something interactive and delicious Date nights — quirky, fun, and plenty of good food Birthday celebrations and small group outings Local students, grad students, alums, and neighbors who want to see a new side of Harvard!

description: Students can expect a high-energy, joyful African and Caribbean dance-fitness experience that combines easy-to-follow choreography, rhythmic movement, cardio, and culturally inspired dance styles. Sylver’s teaching philosophy is rooted in creating a welcoming, judgment-free environment where students can connect with the music, move freely, build confidence, and have fun while getting a great workout. African and Caribbean dance traditions are rooted in the diverse cultures of countries such as Madagascar, Senegal, Ghana, Nigeria, Côte d’Ivoire, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Haiti, Jamaica, Trinidad & Tobago, and Cuba, among many others. The movement and rhythms represented in ’Froca Fitness draw inspiration from forms such as Malagasy dance, Sabar, Azonto, Kizomba, Coupé-Décalé, Ndombolo, Afrobeats, Dancehall, Soca, Kompa, and traditional Haitian rhythms, reflecting generations of African and Caribbean cultural expression, resilience, and exchange. ’Froca Fitness honors this legacy by bringing these influences into a contemporary, high-energy dance-fitness experience that celebrates the diversity and global impact of Afro-diasporic movement and music. title: TRAD & DENTATA
description: TRAD & DENTATA TRAD is a theatrical tear-down of the modern phenomenon of trad—or traditional—wives and the associated Christian nationalist arsenal of beliefs, which also indulges our collective yearning for fantasies of escape. This trad wife is eternally rotund with her husband’s seed: What could possibly shake the ripeness of her faith in this idyllic existence! POV: Your husband is on his way home from work. You’ve got seven buns on the counter and one more in the oven, all baked from scratch, waiting for him. The peaches are bursting on the branches of your homestead’s orchard, while below ground, something is nearing completion. You hear capital H-I-M whisper through the prairie grasses a song that melts your obstinate will, beckoning you to enter a wonderland of reliance and submission. TRAD is directed by Iris McCloughan (Sad Boys in Harpy Land, Lempicka) and was initially co-directed/devised with Meaghan Robichaud ( MEOW!, Meaghan Robichaud is the Greatest Show on Earth ). Written and performed by Hannah Mitchell. “Mitchell does some absolutely wacky shit here…I howled…Praise be.” -Staff Picks “Mitchell’s performance is laugh-out-loud funny…it’s in these moments of audience interaction that Mitchell is at her funniest. Members of the audience are pulled onstage several times during TRAD, and each time is a treat. The writer/actor’s physical and improv comedy skills are so polished.” – Broad Street Review DENTATA: New work from an award-winning idiot. Join Beth Anne (a woman!), a middle-aged beauty queen (almost!), who has spent her life shape shifting into what she thinks others want, only to realize she doesn’t know herself at all. She looks for her reflection in Medusa, the Sirens of The Odyssey, and the Weird Sisters of Macbeth. These misunderstood women (women!) pull her through the wreckage of her past, forcing her to confront the stories she’s been told about what it means to be beautiful, desirable, good, and worthy. title: Beginner and Intermediate Tap for All Levels
description: Classes teach Broadway style tap and focus on repetitive technique to encourage muscle memory and the confidence to create clear sounds. Inclusion is a priority so that all students feel welcome. Classes are “drop-in”, meaning you may join any week and there’s no “semester” commitment. Past steps are always reviewed with the introduction of 1 or 2 new steps or combos each class. Similar to a yoga class, students work at their own individual levels and build up skill at their own pace. Beginners will feel comfortable regardless of when they join. Cost: $20 for 1 hour *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. Registration: Email or text Christina Harrington to register: charrington9901@gmail.com | (617) 852-6240 Pre-registration is encouraged but not required. Drop-ins are welcome. Accepted Payments: Cash, Venmo (@christina-harrington-7) What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Tap dancing began as an answer to the horrors of colonial enslavement…with no musical instruments, Irish and West African slaves turned to their own feet to create rhythms and percussion while pulling movement and technique from traditional tribal and cultural dances. Sounds were initially made with wooden soles, then pennies and bottle caps, finally becoming the modern metal plates screwed to the ball and heel of the shoes. These dances made their way to minstrel and vaudeville shows, eventually transforming into the broadway and rhythm style tap dancing we know today. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? Christina Harrington joined The Dance Complex as a Teaching Artist in May 2012. title: Man of Iron
description: Directed by Andrzej Wajda, 1981. “Why don’t you make a film about us? Call it: Man of Iron .” Wajda’s incendiary sequel to Man of Marble emerged after the director’s encounter with shipyard workers in Gdańsk, where a 1980 strike led to the establishment of Solidarity—Poland’s first independent trade union. Real-life organizers Lech Wałęsa and Anna Walentynowicz appear as themselves in a rough-and-ready cine-pamphlet shot in the immediate aftermath of (what seemed to be) a victorious direct action. The son of original protagonist Birkut takes center stage in a time-hopping narrative which, like its predecessor, blends fiction and documentary into a potion wholly its own. That the experiment was successful is testified by anecdotes of electrified viewers singing the national anthem after screenings. As a result, Wajda was pleased: “Was the film good or bad? What does it matter? There was no film like it.” Feeling (rightly) endangered, the government quickly ensured no other such work could emerge by imposing harsh martial law for the next two years. Part of the series Once There Was History . Andrzej Wajda at 100. Screening on film.

description: $15 @ the door / $10 students / 8:30 start / 8pm doors / seated Jerry Bergonzi , Tenor Saxophone Luther Gray , Drums Plamen Karadonev, Piano Sean Farias, Bass Special Guest , Trumpet A fine, high-powered tenor saxophonist with a tone influenced by John Coltrane, a mastery of chord changes, and a strong musical imagination, Jerry Bergonzi has long had an underground following in the Boston area. He started on clarinet when he was eight, switching to alto at 12, and finally to tenor two years later. Bergonzi was inspired early on by Sonny Rollins, Coltrane, and Hank Mobley. He attended Lowell University and then after graduation played electric bass in local bands behind singers and strippers, saving up enough money to move to New York in 1972. After struggling in the Big Apple for seven years and gaining some recognition as a member of Two Generations of Brubeck and of the Dave Brubeck Quartet (with whom he appeared on several Concord albums during 1979-1981), Bergonzi moved back to Boston in 1981, where he developed a strong career both as a tenorman and as an educator. He has since led several groups (including two called Con Brio and Gonz) and recorded for the Plug, Not Fat, Red, and Blue Note labels. — By Scott Yanow, AllMusic Continuing Every Monday at 8:30pm Lineup subject to change

Bassist Appleman left the band in 1985 to become Chairman of the Bass Department at Berklee College and was replaced by veteran bassist John Lockwood . Bob Gullotti passed away in 2020 and is remembered as one of the greatest jazz drummers of his generation. Francisco Mela, now on drums, graciously fills the space Bob left behind. Along with their impressive tenure with The Fringe, Garzone, Lockwood, and Mela are in great demand as session players and have played with many of the greats of contemporary jazz. Along with keeping up with a busy performance schedule, each of them are well-respected educators helping to inspire the jazz musicians of tomorrow. title: Online Seminar On Undergraduate Mathematics Education
description: Speaker: Nathan Alexander (Howard University) Title: critstats: Reimagining introductory statistics using a critical quantitative approach Abstract: I describe a modern approach to teaching introductory statistics that leverages logic, theory, and computational methods to engage students in critical quantitative analysis. I explore how integrating open-source software tools into this curriculum enables learners to participate in an interdisciplinary process of knowledge construction: defining terms and propositions and applying statistical concepts to social issues. I then discuss the structure of a related package, critstats, which informs a community model and framework for developing informational data systems through which users can examine niche histories, issues, and challenges. title: Four Paintings, Four Stories, Four Uncharted Points in the History of European Painting (Off-Site)
description: The 2026 Annual Henri Zerner Lecture Join us for the Annual Henri Zerner Lecture, which will be held at Harvard’s Department of History of Art and Architecture, across the street from the Harvard Art Museums. Metropolitan Museum of Art curator Stephan Wolohojian, who is the former Landon and Lavinia Clay Curator and head of the Division of European and American Art at the Harvard Art Museums, will deliver this year’s lecture. Museums acquire works of art not only to expand and strengthen their collections, but also to reshape the narratives those collections make possible. The greatest excitement comes with the acquisition of previously unknown or unpublished works, whose emergence can alter established understandings of artistic practice, historical chronology, and cultural context. This lecture examines four paintings that were unknown until their recent acquisition by the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Rather than simply augmenting the historical record, these works invite a fundamental reconsideration of an artist, a period, and the wider cultural world in which they were made. Speaker:Stephan Wolohojian, John Pope-Hennessy Curator in Charge, Department of European Paintings, The Metropolitan Museum of Art This program is sponsored by Harvard’s Department of History of Art and Architecture and the Harvard Art Museums and through the generosity of alumni and friends in establishing the Henri Zerner Lecture Fund.

title: Love Has Come: A Holiday Variety Show at Club Passim
description: This December, a group of Greater-Boston songwriters, musicians, and friends come together at Passim for a one-night-only holiday variety show celebrating original music, collaboration, and a shared love of Amy Grant’s 1983 classic A Christmas Album. With Emily Haviland curating and leading the group,the showcase will feature songwriters such as Alisa Amador, Kaiti Jones, and Hayley Sabella. The Houseband will include Felix Sartori (formerly of Twisted Pine) and Rich Hinman (currently touring with Sara Bareilles). The evening will move between original songs, unexpected collaborations, and selections from A Christmas Album —reimagined by some of New England’s most distinctive voices and players. Part songwriter round, part holiday special, and part gathering of friends, the show trades the usual holiday concert polish for something more intimate, playful, and homespun. Expect artists sitting in on one another’s songs, new arrangements, a few surprises, and plenty of reasons to settle in for the beginning of December. Come celebrate the season with a night of original music, old favorites, and a little Tennessee Christmas in Cambridge.

Majestic Healing Pathways™ is the foundational care model that guides all of Majestic Community Wellness’s programs. title: Intermediate/Advanced Ballet with Dean Vollick
description: Class begins with a thorough set of exercises at the barre that last from 30 to 45 minutes. Centre practice follows, and may consist of a battement tendu exercise, a battement jeté exercise, a grand battement exercise, small and/or large adage, stationary turns, traveling turns, and petite and grand allegro enchaînement (small and big jumps). Classes are structured so that the dancer warms up their feet, legs, hips and upper body gradually. As class progresses there are more changes of weight and eventually, sudden changes of direction. Live music is provided by a pianist, that ranges from classical pieces to selections from ballet repertoire to improvisational contemporary music. Cost: $20 Single Class | $15.00 barre | 5-class package $90.00 *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. Please register in studio with the class assistant Accepted Payments: Cash, Check, Venmo What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Ballet originated in the Italian Renaissance courts around 1500 as large balls or spectacles that were performed by members of the royal court. The French king, Louis XIV, created the first academy and the positions, steps, and movements of the ballet were collected and codified. The spectacles began to be performed by artists that were trained in the academy, originally as part of an opera, and later as ballets that told a story through music, mime, and dance. Over the centuries ballet has influenced folk dance styles of many (mainly European) nations and, more recently, has been influenced by folk, modern, and contemporary forms of dance from all countries. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I had a professional dance career that spanned more than twenty years and included company work in both ballet and contemporary companies as well as dancing, choreographing, and teaching as a freelance artist.

title: SCSB Colloquium Series with Dr. Kuan Hong Wang: Neuromodulation of Circuit Plasticity: From Adaptive Behavior to Precision Therapeutics
description: Date: Wednesday, December 2, 2026 Location: 46-3002 (Singleton Auditorium) Time: 4:00pm-5:00pm ET, followed by reception Speaker: Kuan Hong Wang, Ph.D. Affiliation: Dean’s Professor of Neuroscience, University of Rochester Medical Center Host: Dr. Fan Wang Talk title: Neuromodulation of Circuit Plasticity: From Adaptive Behavior to Precision Therapeutics Abstract: How do neural circuits maintain stable function while remaining flexible enough to adapt? This fundamental question lies at the heart of cognitive flexibility, learning, and resilience across the lifespan. In this lecture, I will discuss how neuromodulatory systems—including dopaminergic, cannabinoid, and neuroimmune signaling—provide the molecular and circuit logic that governs plasticity across development, experience, and disease. Integrating genetic circuit mapping, in vivo imaging, electrophysiology, molecular profiling, and causal circuit manipulation, I will present recent work uncovering how neuromodulators reshape neural circuits across multiple timescales to support adaptive behavior. Finally, I will highlight emerging cross-species approaches, from mice to non-human primates, that enable conserved principles of circuit plasticity to be tested across species and translated toward precision therapeutics. Together, these studies illustrate how deciphering the logic of adaptive behavior can guide the development of selective circuit-based therapies for brain disorders.

title: Lie Groups Seminar
description: Speaker: Siyan Daniel Li-Huerta (MIT) Title: A global Fargues–Fontaine curve Abstract: The "fundamental curve" of arithmetic over nonarchimedean local fields is the Fargues–Fontaine curve. You'd think the "fundamental curve" of arithmetic over global function fields is. just the associated curve over $\mathbb{F}_q$. In this talk, I will instead advocate for a different "curve", in the spirit of the Fargues–Fontaine curve. I will explain how its moduli stack of bundles is the function field analog of Igusa stacks, as well as the perspective it gives on Langlands duality.

Linear Salsa is a hybrid dance that comes from Mambo (a Cuban style that was popularized in the 1950’s NYC Palladium). NY Mambo is a marriage of footwork and partner-work from Cuba (Aftro-Cuban movements, Cuban Son) and the U.S. (Jazz, Swing). description: The goal of this class is to build technical competence through drills and choreographies as well as self-expression, musicality, fluidity, and stamina. Samba is a rhythm and a dance that exudes equal parts beauty, spirituality, and resistance. Borne in Brazil from enslaved Africans, samba has spread to the mainstream and is now one of the country’s most famous exports. Samba is constantly evolving in all of its forms; currently there are many popular samba sub-genres, including pagode, samba rock, bossa nova, etc. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? SambaViva teachers have a minimum of 5 (and as many as 20!) years dancing and training samba and other Brazilian styles. All have trained closely with Brazilian instructors both intensively and over many years. Our regular instructors have traveled extensively in the country to study dance but also to participate in the culture, learn the language, and explore the many sites and experiences Brazil has to offer. Finish this statement: I am passionate about teaching this style because… …Samba is contagious! How can students learn more about this offering? description: Join us for a special conversation with author Ted Chiang and MIT President Sally Kornbluth about Exhalation. President Kornbluth has chosen Chiang’s celebrated science fiction short story collection to celebrate 10 years of MIT Reads. Exploring the book’s provocative questions about technology and humanity, their discussion will focus on the stories "The Truth of Fact, the Truth of Feeling,” "The Lifecycle of Software Objects,” “Omphalos,” “What’s Expected of Us," and "Exhalation." In this fantastical and elegant collection, Chiang wrestles with the oldest questions on Earth – What is the nature of the universe? What does it mean to be human? – and ones that no one else has even imagined. And, each in its own way, the stories prove that complex and thoughtful science fiction can rise to new heights of beauty, meaning, and compassion. This event is part of MIT Reads, a program that embraces the power of reading and storytelling to cultivate social connection, individual reflection, and a sense of our shared humanity. Designed to foster empathy, curiosity, and belonging, MIT Reads brings together the campus community – and readers everywhere – through common reading experiences, author talks, and group discussions. -- This hybrid event is free and open to all, but pre-registration is required. For online participants, the URL will be emailed closer to the event. Accessibility: Our events are enriched by your presence, and we are committed to making them accessible. title: Michael Bravata: “The Montcalms” Release Show
description: Michael Bravata: “The Montcalms” Release Show Celebrating the release of his 2026 album The Montcalms , Michael Bravata will perform the record live in its entirety, backed by a full band, including a strings section. Musicians who helped record the album will join him on stage to recreate its fully acoustic, all-natural instrumentation at The Rockwell. Michael Bravata is a Boston-based experimental guitarist and composer who has spent his career creating a catalog of evocative and immersive avant-garde pieces. Born in Texas, Michael spent his formative years in the vibrant indie music scenes of Dallas and Austin. While pursuing a degree at UTA, Michael wrote and created music driven through post-rock and drone genres. Over the past decade, Michael’s insatiable appetite for artistic exploration and growth has led him to the experimental world of ambient landscapes. This shift marked an evolution in his music, reflecting a deeper examination of acoustic textures and immersive atmospheres. Michael’s writing is contemplative, blending the introspective nature of indie rock with ambient’s boundless creativity. In 2024, Michael completed a Composing and Orchestrating for Film and Television certificate at the Berklee College of Music. This leap has further pushed his pursuits by incorporating orchestral and traditional instrumentation into his work. title: ChemE Dept. Seminar: Dissipative Self-Assembly of Colloidal Suspensions in Microgravity
description: Speaker: Eric M. Furst, Professor of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering; University of Delaware I will describe experiments performed in the Microgravity Science Glovebox aboard the International Space Station. Because the gravitational Péclet number scales as the fourth power of aggregate size, even small density mismatches drive sedimentation on Earth once particles begin to cluster; microgravity removes this and allows direct observation of fully three-dimensional assembly. Across 96 flight test points spanning field strength, toggle frequency, and duty ratio, we find six characteristic structural regimes: structureless suspensions, an arrested gel-like network, sheets, ribbons, a spiky phase, and a transient fluid-fluid state. Quantitative image analysis of domain elongation, surface texture, and interaggregate separation yields a state diagram organized by a dissipative timescale, and a duty-ratio-weighted magnetostatic energy scale — axes suggested by the toggled-interaction theory of Sherman and Swan, and which also organize data from two earlier ISS campaigns. I will close with reflections on three ISS campaigns spanning more than twenty years — what microgravity can access, a few of the unique challenges, and what it is like to run an experiment through a crew member in orbit.

title: Christy Scott Cashman at Harvard Book Store
description: Harvard Book Store welcomes Christy Scott Cashman —best-selling and award-winning author, actress, producer, and the founder of the nonprofit YouthINK—for a discussion of her new novel, What Happened in Beulah . About What Happened in Beulah A teenage girl uncovers the dark secrets of her Smoky Mountain town while searching for a missing classmate in this gripping coming-of-age mystery perfect for fans of Where the Crawdads Sing . Nestled in the foothills of the Smoky Mountains, Beulah has always seemed steady—rooted in tradition, shaped by generations, and slow to change. But in 1986, the ground has shifted, and no one feels that more than fifteen-year-old Barrett Childress Owens. Between her parents’ unraveling marriage and a school full of kids she can’t connect with, she feels invisible in her own hometown. When Lacy Gunderson, the captivating new girl everyone is curious about, suddenly vanishes, the town’s calm surface fractures. Search parties comb the woods. A police investigation begins. Rumors multiply. Families close ranks. And Barrett begins to sense how much the adults around her choose not to say. As Beulah clings to its usual rituals—including the annual Miss Kudzu pageant, which has shaped local girlhood for decades—Barrett is forced to navigate a community where loss lingers in the air and secrets are carefully kept. Her journey through the uncertainty reshapes her understanding of friendships, family, and the complex place she calls home. A rich coming-of-age story with a pulse of mystery and a budding romance, What Happened in Beulah explores the fault lines of a small town and the courage it takes to face the truths people would rather bury.

Flamenco is a form of song, dance, and instrumental (mostly guitar) music commonly associated with the Andalusian Roma (Gypsies) of southern Spain. (There, the Roma people are called Gitanos.) The roots of flamenco, though somewhat mysterious, seem to lie in the Roma migration from Rajasthan (in northwest India) to Spain between the 9th and 14th centuries. These migrants brought with them musical instruments, such as tambourines, bells, and wooden castanets, and an extensive repertoire of songs and dances. In Spain they encountered the rich cultures of the Sephardic Jews and the Moors. Their centuries-long cultural intermingling produced the unique art form known as flamenco. (https://www.britannica.com/art/flamenco) What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? description: Harvard Book Store welcomes Stephen Kinzer —award-winning writer and correspondent, and Senior Fellow at the Watson Institute for International and Public Affairs at Brown University—for a discussion of his new book, Boiling Point: How America Brought War to Ukraine. About Boiling Point From bestselling author Stephen Kinzer, the untold history of America’s secret seventy-five-year struggle in Ukraine that set the stage for today’s war. The war in Ukraine has dominated world headlines for nearly four years. It caught most people by surprise. Until the Russian invasion in February 2022, few Americans even knew where Ukraine was. Once the fighting began, however, support for its cause surged instinctively–Russia was the aggressor, Ukraine its victim. Yet the war did not explode out of nowhere. For seventy-five years, Moscow and Washington fought over Ukraine in the most sustained covert conflict in modern history. Both sides wanted to keep it hidden. They succeeded–until now. In this groundbreaking book, Stephen Kinzer tells that story for the first time. Beginning in the refugee camps of postwar Europe, where CIA officers recruited Ukrainians to infiltrate their homeland, it follows generations of rebels, exiles, traitors, and covert operatives through decades of clandestine missions. Nearly all of those early fighters were captured or killed, yet the CIA never gave up. From the late 1940s through the end of the Cold War, American leaders saw Ukrainians as their most effective weapon against Moscow, and they continued to press that strategy after Ukraine’s independence, especially as NATO expanded eastward. Richly detailed and plot-driven, Boiling Point shows how the United States made Ukraine its most important European project of the twenty-first century, culminating in the Maidan uprising of 2014 and the escalation that led to war. description: Beginner House introduces students to house music, and house dance fundamentals. No experience is required! One of the world’s most popular music genres, “house” is an electronic dance music genre that emerged in Chicago in the late 70s/early 80s following the disco era. The term “house” was derived from The Warehouse, a Chicago club where the music was often played. Though the essence of the dance is purely freestyle, popular steps performed in NYC dance clubs were eventually recognized as “house dance foundation.” Members of NYC’s Dance Fusion were the first to teach house dance, which contributed greatly to house becoming a worldwide phenomenon. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? A master Taekwondo-ist and professional dancer, Sean began dancing in the year 2000, and was formally introduced to house dance by Boston native Ricardo Foster Jr in 2007. For years, Sean sought opportunities to learn from and train under many house dance teachers including Jardy Santiago, members of NYC’s Dance Fusion, and Edson Gonzaga who helped unlock Sean’s understanding of house music and develop his own personal dance style. description: 19th Annual Herb Pomeroy Memorial Concert—Giant Steps in Jazz MIT Festival Jazz Ensemble Special guest: Trombonist Elliot Mason Friday, November 13, 2027, 8:00pmLinde Music Building, Thomas Tull Concert Hall, MIT$20 general admission, Free for MIT Community Get Tickets Here MIT Festival Jazz Ensemble, Frederick Harris, Jr., Music Director collaborates with special guest trombonist Elliot Mason for MIT’s 19th annual celebration of Herb Pomeroy (1930-2007), “the father of jazz at MIT,” the MIT Festival Jazz Ensemble (MIT FJE). This special concert includes music of Ellington, Coltrane, Chick Corea, Miguel Zenón and others. Elliot Mason is an internationally acclaimed trombonist, composer, educator, and bass trumpet specialist. For more than two decades, he has been a member of the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra under the direction of Wynton Marsalis and performs regularly with the Wynton Marsalis Septet. Alongside his work with Jazz at Lincoln Center, Mason leads his own Quintet, co-leads the Mason Brothers Quintet with his brother, Brad Mason, and performs with the Sofijazz Quintet. An accomplished educator, Mason has served on the jazz faculty at The Juilliard School since 2016, as their Jazz Trombone Instructor, Studio Class Resident Artist, and Brass Mentor. Throughout his career, he has performed with many of jazz's most celebrated ensembles, including the Count Basie Orchestra, the Mingus Big Band, the Maria Schneider Orchestra, Maynard Ferguson's Big Bop Nouveau, and the Toshiko Akiyoshi Orchestra. As a featured performer and collaborator, Mason has shared the stage with an extraordinary range of artists, including Paul Simon, Wayne Shorter, Branford Marsalis, Chick Corea, Kenny Garrett, Bobby Hutcherson, Ahmad Jamal, Chucho Valdés, Chano Domínguez, Chris Potter, Randy Brecker, Joe Lovano, Carl Fontana, and Bill Watrous. title: Eliza Edens & Nora Meier
description: $12 advance / $15 day of show / 9:15 doors / 9:30 music / all ages Brooklyn-based songwriter Eliza Edens celebrates the release of their latest record 'Death Drive.' Local songwriter Nora Meier supports. Eliza Edens is a Brooklyn-based songwriter who writes songs that dance inside the white-hot intersection of pleasure and pain. Bold and sincere, their songs are like antique cameo necklaces–snapshots of tenderness, worn close to the heart. A palette of punchy electric guitars and drums, gentle keys, and flourishes of saxophone and electronic percussion accent Edens’ voice as they sing of lovers & lilacs, grief & gratitude, and Freud’s “death drive.” Chameleonic in nature, Edens touches corners of pop, rock, folk, and country–with their voice as the glue that binds each genre foray together into a commanding sound. Edens came up initially on the DIY songwriter circuit–playing self-booked tours of small clubs and listening rooms on the quiet success of 2020’s Time Away From Time and 2022’s lush acoustic-fingerpicked We’ll Become the Flowers . They earned praise from outlets such as Paste Magazine, The Nashville Scene, Spill Magazine, and Americana UK while incessantly touring across America. Cutting their teeth on the road eventually paid off as Edens won runner-up at the esteemed Telluride Troubadour Songwriting competition in 2024. The veneer of a quiet songster singing breezy Nick Drake-esque melodies was quickly dashed after Edens lost their mother in late 2024 after a long journey with early-onset dementia. Tap dancing began as an answer to the horrors of colonial enslavement…with no musical instruments, Irish and West African slaves turned to their own feet to create rhythms and percussion while pulling movement and technique from traditional tribal and cultural dances. Sounds were initially made with wooden soles, then pennies and bottle caps, finally becoming the modern metal plates screwed to the ball and heel of the shoes. These dances made their way to minstrel and vaudeville shows, eventually transforming into the broadway and rhythm style tap dancing we know today. title: The Conductor
description: Directed by Andrzej Wajda, 1980. In interviews, Wajda often identified as a musical layman, alleging he “prefers silence.” Yet The Conductor , an exemplar of Poland’s "cinema of moral concern,” dramatizes the world of classical music with ease. Working for the first (and last) time in America, the director activated English stage titan John Gielgud as John/Jan Lasocki, a prewar emigrant who enjoys conductorial fame in New York. Wajda regulars Andrzej Seweryn and Krystyna Janda act as maestro and violinist in a provincial philharmonic undone by the arrival of mythic Lasocki after decades abroad. Released just after Fellini’s Orchestra Rehearsal , the film marks a high point of Wajda’s ’70 allegoricism, the intra-ensemble authority struggle widely interpreted as a microcosm of Polish politics at the time. (“The orchestra is a society that accepts one leader but not another,” Wajda observed.) The Conductor was a favorite of Ingmar Bergman, who would have also appreciated the stylization of Gielgud as something of a stand-in for then newly-elected Pope John Paul II. Part of the series Once There Was History . Andrzej Wajda at 100.

title: Jerry Bergonzi Quartet
description: $15 @ the door / $10 students / 8:30 start / 8pm doors / seated Jerry Bergonzi , Tenor Saxophone Luther Gray , Drums Plamen Karadonev, Piano Sean Farias, Bass Special Guest , Trumpet A fine, high-powered tenor saxophonist with a tone influenced by John Coltrane, a mastery of chord changes, and a strong musical imagination, Jerry Bergonzi has long had an underground following in the Boston area. He started on clarinet when he was eight, switching to alto at 12, and finally to tenor two years later. Bergonzi was inspired early on by Sonny Rollins, Coltrane, and Hank Mobley. He attended Lowell University and then after graduation played electric bass in local bands behind singers and strippers, saving up enough money to move to New York in 1972. After struggling in the Big Apple for seven years and gaining some recognition as a member of Two Generations of Brubeck and of the Dave Brubeck Quartet (with whom he appeared on several Concord albums during 1979-1981), Bergonzi moved back to Boston in 1981, where he developed a strong career both as a tenorman and as an educator. He has since led several groups (including two called Con Brio and Gonz) and recorded for the Plug, Not Fat, Red, and Blue Note labels. — By Scott Yanow, AllMusic Continuing Every Monday at 8:30pm Lineup subject to change

title: EconLOL: an Economics-Themed Comedy Show
description: EconLOL: an Economics-Themed Comedy Show EconLOL is the world’s first, best, and only economics-themed powerpoint comedy variety show. A monthly live show in NYC, this is EconLOL ’s Boston debut. Comedian and Economist Luke Strathmann takes on the world of economics with a whirlwind show. He will reveal the secrets that economists have been holding from us since Adam Smith first put pen to paper, whlie addressing some of the greatest economic questions of our time: Where does money come from? Why are movies so expensive? How on earth did someone sell a Beanie Baby for seven million dollars? Why was that person not him? ARTIST BIO: Luke Strathmann runs the communications team at Yale’s Department of Economics, where he’s Editor-in-Chief of the Yale Economics Magazine. He’s previously worked for MIT and Princeton’s economics departments, the World Bank, the UN, Omidyar Network, and the AI Now Institute. His humor writing has appeared in The New Yorker and McSweeney’s, and he performs comedy at clubs all around NYC. He is the host of EconLOL , the world’s first, best, and only live economics-themed comedy show. description: Fundamentals 1A assumes no dance experience at all, and will teach the fundamental connection techniques for partnered Balboa dancing, along with the primary figures of Balboa, and Fundamentals 1B refines those techniques and adds a few more figures. Class is taught ELEF (Everybody Leads Everybody Follows), which helps you better understand how both roles work and feel, so that beyond this series, you can choose the one that suits you, or choose to keep dancing in both! Balboa is a vernacular swing dance from Southern California in the 1920s and 30s, and is indebted to the African-American roots and culture of Swing Jazz and Swing dancing. We encourage everyone to explore the history of this dance, the dancers that created it in Southern California, and the music and musicians that made it possible. Balboa today is an improvisational, joyful partner dance with a vibrant worldwide community, evolving into the present while honoring its origins. title: Intermediate/Advanced Ballet with Dean Vollick
description: Class begins with a thorough set of exercises at the barre that last from 30 to 45 minutes. Centre practice follows, and may consist of a battement tendu exercise, a battement jeté exercise, a grand battement exercise, small and/or large adage, stationary turns, traveling turns, and petite and grand allegro enchaînement (small and big jumps). Classes are structured so that the dancer warms up their feet, legs, hips and upper body gradually. As class progresses there are more changes of weight and eventually, sudden changes of direction. Live music is provided by a pianist, that ranges from classical pieces to selections from ballet repertoire to improvisational contemporary music. Cost: $20 Single Class | $15.00 barre | 5-class package $90.00 *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. Please register in studio with the class assistant Accepted Payments: Cash, Check, Venmo What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Ballet originated in the Italian Renaissance courts around 1500 as large balls or spectacles that were performed by members of the royal court. The French king, Louis XIV, created the first academy and the positions, steps, and movements of the ballet were collected and codified. The spectacles began to be performed by artists that were trained in the academy, originally as part of an opera, and later as ballets that told a story through music, mime, and dance. Over the centuries ballet has influenced folk dance styles of many (mainly European) nations and, more recently, has been influenced by folk, modern, and contemporary forms of dance from all countries. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I had a professional dance career that spanned more than twenty years and included company work in both ballet and contemporary companies as well as dancing, choreographing, and teaching as a freelance artist.

title: Multi-Site Exhibition Tour: Alfonso Ossorio: Line and Lineage and Knowledge Is Myth: Chimeric Continuities
description: Join Ally Cirelli, curator of Alfonso Ossorio: Line and Lineage (October 23, 2026–April 11, 2027) at the Harvard Art Museums, and Danni Shen, curator of Knowledge Is Myth: Chimeric Continuities (October 1–December 13, 2026) at the Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts, for a multi-site tour of the two interconnected exhibitions. At the Harvard Art Museums exhibition, we will explore the experimental processes of modern artist Alfonso Ossorio and work by contemporary artists Enzo Camacho and Ami Lien that respond to his artistic legacy in the Philippines. Continuing to the Carpenter Center, we will view more works by Ossorio, Camacho, and Lien as well as other contemporary artists working with mythology. Throughout the tour, Cirelli and Shen will highlight the intergenerational connections made by these artists through material experimentation. Led by:Ally Cirelli, Cunningham Senior Curatorial Assistant for the Collection, Division of Modern and Contemporary Art, Harvard Art Museums Danni Shen, Senior Curatorial and Public Programs Assistant, Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts Alfonso Ossorio: Line and Lineage is made possible through the generous support of the Ossorio Fund, with additional support from the Recharge Foundation Fund for Contemporary Art. , Fund for Modern and Contemporary Art.

title: The Material Culture of Islamic Calligraphy
description: The 2026 Norma Jean Calderwood Lecture Calligraphy is the most recognizable of Islamic arts, and it is often seen in its finished form—an inscription written on paper; carved in stone, wood, or ivory; cast in metal; or woven into fabric. Yet calligraphy always begins as a trace left by a pen, a practice sustained by a rich material culture. Cultural historian İrvin Cemil Schick looks at the wide array of tools used in the artistic practice of Islamic calligraphy, such as reed pens, penknives, cutting boards, inks, inkwells, papers, and scissors. Speaker:İrvin Cemil Schick, Cultural historian İrvin Cemil Schick is a cultural and intellectual historian specializing in the Ottoman Empire. He holds Ph.D.s from MIT and the École des Hautes Études en Sciences Sociales, in Paris, and has taught at Harvard University, MIT, and Istanbul Şehir University. He has also held guest positions at Boston University, Sabancı University, Boğaziçi University, and the University of Massachusetts, Amherst. His principal research interests include the Islamic arts of the book, particularly calligraphy, illumination, and marbling; gender, sexuality, spatiality, and the body in Islam; animals and the environment in Islam; and occult practices in Islam. This event is part of In Conversation, a series of evening programs that feature local and international curators, artists, scholars, and more. Running from September through April, these events highlight our temporary exhibitions, permanent collections, and a range of creative voices.

Linear Salsa is a hybrid dance that comes from Mambo (a Cuban style that was popularized in the 1950’s NYC Palladium). description: Beginner House introduces students to house music, and house dance fundamentals. No experience is required! One of the world’s most popular music genres, “house” is an electronic dance music genre that emerged in Chicago in the late 70s/early 80s following the disco era. The term “house” was derived from The Warehouse, a Chicago club where the music was often played. Though the essence of the dance is purely freestyle, popular steps performed in NYC dance clubs were eventually recognized as “house dance foundation.” Members of NYC’s Dance Fusion were the first to teach house dance, which contributed greatly to house becoming a worldwide phenomenon. title: In-Person Bellydance
description: In this class, you’ll explore earthy Egyptian, Turkish, and American style movements, dynamic combinations, and expressive choreography blending tradition and innovation. Experience the power of fiery hip-locks and shimmies, and the fluid beauty of serpentine undulations. Drawing from decades of study with master teachers and over thirty years of performance experience, Johara offers expert guidance in a supportive, inspiring environment—honoring the depth of this ancient art while inviting each student to discover their own unique style within it. Instructions: Wear comfortable dance or workout clothing that allows you to move freely. Classes are danced barefoot or in dance shoes. Students will be encouraged to acquire a veil and finger cymbals (zsagaat/ills). Cash preferred, or Venmo Drop-ins always welcome! What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? The more authentic name for this dance form is raqs sharqi (“dance of the East”), and its roots lie in the Middle and Near East, primarily in Egypt and Turkey. This dance form was introduced to the United States and Europe at the turn of the 20th century, but it was not widely performed or taught until the 1950s and 1960s, when the belly dance craze swept across the U.S. The American cabaret style of belly dance is rooted in the legacy passed down by notable American teachers and performers, who blended Middle Eastern influences with their own innovations and movement styles drawn from diverse dance backgrounds. title: Tony Trischka’s Holiday Show: Of A Winter’s Night at Club Passim
description: Tony Trischka is considered to be the consummate banjo artist and perhaps the most influential banjo player in the roots music world. For more than 45 years, his stylings have inspired a whole generation of bluegrass and acoustic musicians with the many voices he has brought to the instrument. A native of Syracuse, New York, Trischka’s interest in banjo was sparked by the Kingston Trio’s “Charlie and the MTA” in 1963. Two years later, he joined the Down City Ramblers, where he remained through 1971. That year, Trischka made his recording debut on 15 Bluegrass Instrumentals with the band Country Cooking; at the same time, he was also a member of America’s premier sports-rock band Country Granola. In 1973, he began a three-year stint with Breakfast Special. Between 1974 and 1975, he recorded two solo albums, Bluegrass Light and Heartlands. After one more solo album in 1976, Banjoland, he went on to become musical leader for the Broadway show The Robber Bridegroom. With his fearless musical curiosity as the guiding force, Tony Trischka’s critically acclaimed release, Territory roams widely through the banjo’s creative terrain. Nine selections partner Tony with fellow banjoists Pete Seeger, Mike Seeger, Bill Evans, Bill Keith and Bruce Molsky.

title: Queer Dance Party with DeVante Love
description: Queer people have long used song and dance to find the joy and resilience needed to navigate oppressive forces that refuse to accept us. The queer dance party is an extension of that lineage. Together, we let the entrancing sounds of pop, house, and disco turn our bodies into instruments of joy, love, and ferocity. We begin with a warm-up that loosens the body and summons a fabulous, cunty, ferocious version of yourself. Next, we learn movement drawn from queer dance forms such as vogue, waacking, club dance, house, and martial arts. We close with an extended free dance to express ourselves, build community, and cultivate the mental and emotional fortitude to stay dynamic and fierce in everyday life, no matter what comes. Tickets Soon DEVANTE LOVE: DeVante Love (they/them) is an Afroindigiqueer dance scholar-artist, therapist turned medicinewoman, and lay Buddhist/Daoist monk. Their performance work supports healing and empowerment through medicine dances and warrior dances that incorporate martial arts, queer dance aesthetics, dance therapy, and ecoshamanism. They have been training and teaching this work for 20 years and have spent the past 6 years performing this work on stages across the U.S., East Asia, and East Africa. title: Without Anesthesia, aka Rough Treatment
description: Directed by Andrzej Wajda, 1978. War correspondent Jerzy returns to Warsaw, says the wrong thing on TV, and watches powerlessly as his career, relationship and reputation disintegrate. The first of five Wajda screenplays written by Agnieszka Holland, Without Anesthesia loosely adapts the travails of journalist Ryszard Kapuściński yet treads a claustrophobic, Kafkian path wholly its own. Poland’s cinema of moral unrest meets American paranoid thriller in one man’s odyssey through government systems set to kill. Krystyna Janda excels as wordless student Agata, observing Jerzy’s descent into apathy and alcohol head-on. A worthy successor to 1977’s Man of Marble , the film emerged at a raucous time in Poland’s politics, which is to say at the peak of its political cinema. (Krzysztof Zanussi’s Camouflage and Feliks Falk’s Top Dog both date to 1977-78.) Wajda would return to the 1920s in Maids of Wilko , but not before receiving wide acclaim for the roughness of Without Anesthesia both at home and internationally. Part of the series Once There Was History . Andrzej Wajda at 100.

title: Kenny Raskin: Follow The Laugh
description: Kenny Raskin: Follow The Laugh This workshop is designed for those who yearn to be clowns, or for those who just want to use these skills to enhance their acting chops. Clowns live in a world of spontaneity, flexibility and distractibility. They follow their noses, and the rest of their senses as well. This workshop is designed to help you find the part of yourself that connects you to your physicality and spontaneity, sparking wonderfully creative ideas on stage. To create comedy, one must create surprise. To do that, one must surprise oneself. My students initially work without thought, without ideas, but rather with their direct contact with the world. In this way they learn to create accidents, to see them coming — in a sense, to make them intentional. We also learn to listen to the audience, as they often tell the performer what is happening. That is why I tell my students to “follow the laugh!” If they laugh, something is worth exploring… SOCIAL MEDIA: Facebook: kenny.raskin.7 / Instagram: @kennyraskin / LinkedIn: kennyraskin INSTRUCTOR BIO: For the past forty years, Kenny Raskin has made a name for himself worldwide as a leading physical comedian and teacher of clowning. He starred as the lead clown Everyman in Cirque du Soleil’s NOUVELLE EXPERIENCE, and was also featured in Cirque du Soleil’s 3D IMAX film entitled JOURNEY OF MAN, and appeared as well as the Vaudeville Comedian in director Barry Levinson’s film, LIBERTY HEIGHTS. Kenny also originated the role of Lefou in Disney’s Broadway production of Beauty and the Beast. H e has also been a frequent player in the European Variete and television circuit, performing in theaters such as the WINTERGARTEN VARIETE in Berlin, APOLLO VARIETE in Dusseldorf, the Prinzregenten Theater Munich, and BBC television. Kenny is presently the artistic director of the Boston based Medical Clown Troupe Hearts and Noses. Similar to a yoga class, students work at their own individual levels and build up skill at their own pace. Beginners will feel comfortable regardless of when they join. Tap dancing began as an answer to the horrors of colonial enslavement…with no musical instruments, Irish and West African slaves turned to their own feet to create rhythms and percussion while pulling movement and technique from traditional tribal and cultural dances. Sounds were initially made with wooden soles, then pennies and bottle caps, finally becoming the modern metal plates screwed to the ball and heel of the shoes. These dances made their way to minstrel and vaudeville shows, eventually transforming into the broadway and rhythm style tap dancing we know today. This class is best suited for students with prior experience working with a mantón and will culminate in a performance in the spring. Flamenco is a form of song, dance, and instrumental (mostly guitar) music commonly associated with the Andalusian Roma (Gypsies) of southern Spain. (There, the Roma people are called Gitanos.) The roots of flamenco, though somewhat mysterious, seem to lie in the Roma migration from Rajasthan (in northwest India) to Spain between the 9th and 14th centuries. These migrants brought with them musical instruments, such as tambourines, bells, and wooden castanets, and an extensive repertoire of songs and dances. In Spain they encountered the rich cultures of the Sephardic Jews and the Moors. Their centuries-long cultural intermingling produced the unique art form known as flamenco. (https://www.britannica.com/art/flamenco) What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I have been dancing and performing flamenco professionally for over 30 years. Throughout my career, I was also a member of three local flamenco companies: Ramon de los Reyes Spanish Dance Theatre, Omayra Amaya Flamenco Sin Limites and my own company, Flamenco Dance Project. I have studied both here and in Spain, and continue my studies (to keep current with the dance) at various workshops both here and abroad. title: Fanny and Alexander
description: Directed by Ingmar Bergman, 1982. In 1979, Ingmar Bergman conceived Fanny and Alexander as his swan song, calling it “the sum total of my life as a filmmaker.” The director returned to his own childhood in Uppsala, Sweden, and for the first time, told a story from the perspective of a child, Alexander Ekdahl. The film interrogates family, faith, mortality and—perhaps most importantly—imagination. At its core is the ideological clash between the creative Ekdahl family and their authoritarian bishop stepfather—a figure inspired by Bergman’s own father, a Lutheran minister. Part of the series Nostalgia, A Harvard Undergraduate Cinematheque Program. Screening on film.

Capoeira Angola developed in Brazil from a variety of African roots. N’golo from Angola, rhythms from Congo, and acrobatics from Guinea combined to form a martial art disguised as a dance and played like a game. All these elements plus a deliberate sense of fun result in a vigorous workout for the body and mind! I saw Capoeira played on the streets, and was curious to know more. I fell in love with the music, history, and movements of the style. I graduated as a Mestre in 1984 and moved to Boston in 1986. I was the first to teach Capoeira in New England. Mestre Joao Pequenho certified me as a teacher of Capoeira Angola in 1991. Contra Mestre Calango: I moved to Boston in 2000 to continue training with Mestre Deraldo. Since then, I traveled with him to universities and events around the world to assist in demonstrating and teaching of the beautiful art of Capoeira Angola. I graduated as a Contra Mestre in 2017. title: Unsilent Night at Harvard Square
description: Be a part of the music where Harvard Square is our score! Phil Kline’s Unsilent Night is an original composition written specifically to be heard outdoors in the month of December. It takes the form of a street promenade in which the audience becomes the performer. Each participant gets one of four tracks of music in the form of a cassette, CD, or MP3. Together all four tracks comprise Unsilent Night. The fact that the participants play different “parts” simultaneously helps create the special sound of the piece. Participants carry boomboxes, or anything that amplifies music, and simultaneously start playing the music. Our carefully chosen route through streets of the Square will create a unique mobile sound sculpture which is different from every listener’s perspective. Please join us at 5pm at the corner of Palmer & Church as we begin our stroll through Harvard Square! Gathering will begin at 4:30pm. For details on what to bring, please click here . description: Directed by Andrzej Wajda, 1965. After the remarkable yet underwhelmingly received Samson (1961) and Siberian Lady Macbeth (1962), Wajda continued his cycle of black-and-white CinemaScope features with The Ashes , an adaptation of Stefan Żeromski’s two-volume doorstopper and a product of Polish cinema’s ’60s turn toward high-budget historical epics. (Jerzy Kawalerowicz’s Pharaoh and Wojciech Has’ Saragossa Manuscript are two other examples.) Soon-to-be Wajda regular Daniel Olbrychski shines as Rafał Olbromski, an impoverished nobleman—a reverse Barry Lyndon of sorts—entangled in ever-shifting factions and fronts in the Napoleonic Wars. Characters move in and out of episodic focus as swiftly as they crisscross Jerzy Lipman’s widescreen frame; in microscopically choreographed and costumed combat scenes, over 1,500 bayoneted extras clash on foot and horse, Wajda’s signature lateral tracking shots moving at equestrian speed. While envisioned as an “historical fresco,” the film struck a nerve with Polish nationalists who could not bear the depiction (Wajda’s, but originally Żeromski’s) of Poles as imperfect, manipulable and capable of violence. Part of the series Once There Was History . Andrzej Wajda at 100.

description: Kenny Raskin: Follow The Laugh This workshop is designed for those who yearn to be clowns, or for those who just want to use these skills to enhance their acting chops. Clowns live in a world of spontaneity, flexibility and distractibility. They follow their noses, and the rest of their senses as well. This workshop is designed to help you find the part of yourself that connects you to your physicality and spontaneity, sparking wonderfully creative ideas on stage. To create comedy, one must create surprise. To do that, one must surprise oneself. My students initially work without thought, without ideas, but rather with their direct contact with the world. In this way they learn to create accidents, to see them coming — in a sense, to make them intentional. We also learn to listen to the audience, as they often tell the performer what is happening. That is why I tell my students to “follow the laugh!” If they laugh, something is worth exploring… SOCIAL MEDIA: Facebook: kenny.raskin.7 / Instagram: @kennyraskin / LinkedIn: kennyraskin INSTRUCTOR BIO: For the past forty years, Kenny Raskin has made a name for himself worldwide as a leading physical comedian and teacher of clowning. He starred as the lead clown Everyman in Cirque du Soleil’s NOUVELLE EXPERIENCE, and was also featured in Cirque du Soleil’s 3D IMAX film entitled JOURNEY OF MAN, and appeared as well as the Vaudeville Comedian in director Barry Levinson’s film, LIBERTY HEIGHTS. Kenny also originated the role of Lefou in Disney’s Broadway production of Beauty and the Beast. H e has also been a frequent player in the European Variete and television circuit, performing in theaters such as the WINTERGARTEN VARIETE in Berlin, APOLLO VARIETE in Dusseldorf, the Prinzregenten Theater Munich, and BBC television. Kenny is presently the artistic director of the Boston based Medical Clown Troupe Hearts and Noses. title: Pan Tadeusz, aka The Last Days
description: Directed by Andrzej Wajda, 1999. Amidst social and economic turmoil, 1990s Polish cinema turned toward heritage. Pan Tadeusz —shot in 1998 to mark romantic writer Adam Mickiewicz’s bicentennial—is Andrzej Wajda at his most nation-building and nostalgic. Adapting the eponymous epic poem, Wajda retains its lyric verse, supplementing Mickiewicz’s rhyming couplets with elegantly swaying camera moves. Set in 1811-12 Polish-speaking Lithuania, the film revels in aristocratic quarrels and interdynastic conflict as two families iron out a decades-long feud against the backdrop of Napoleon’s (somewhat eagerly awaited) invasion of Russia. The film was a popular patriotic event of the highest order: over six million tickets were sold at home (the international release was a bomb), garnering Wajda praise for once again uniting a disheveled nation through images. Prizing extravagant theatricality over historical veracity, Pan Tadeusz stands today as one of Wajda’s strongest and strangest costume dramas, its sumptuous CinemaScope photography evincing a desire to depict the past as it never was. Part of the series Once There Was History . Andrzej Wajda at 100. Screening on film.

title: Beginner and Intermediate Tap for All Levels
description: Classes teach Broadway style tap and focus on repetitive technique to encourage muscle memory and the confidence to create clear sounds. Inclusion is a priority so that all students feel welcome. Classes are “drop-in”, meaning you may join any week and there’s no “semester” commitment. Past steps are always reviewed with the introduction of 1 or 2 new steps or combos each class. Similar to a yoga class, students work at their own individual levels and build up skill at their own pace. Beginners will feel comfortable regardless of when they join. Accepted Payments: Cash, Venmo (@christina-harrington-7) What is the legacy of the genre/form/style you are teaching? Tap dancing began as an answer to the horrors of colonial enslavement…with no musical instruments, Irish and West African slaves turned to their own feet to create rhythms and percussion while pulling movement and technique from traditional tribal and cultural dances. Sounds were initially made with wooden soles, then pennies and bottle caps, finally becoming the modern metal plates screwed to the ball and heel of the shoes. These dances made their way to minstrel and vaudeville shows, eventually transforming into the broadway and rhythm style tap dancing we know today. As a child she studied tap, jazz, and ballet at the Paula Coffey Dance Center in East Bridgewater, MA from 1987-1995 where tap was always her favorite. title: Ashes and Diamonds
description: Directed by Andrzej Wajda, 1958. The last and loudest entry in Wajda’s WWII trilogy, Ashes and Diamonds adapts Jerzy Andrzejewski’s eponymous 1948 novel into one of Polish cinema’s strongest and most celebrated works. Set on May 8, 1945—Victory Day in Europe—after Red Army battalions had already expelled the occupier out of Poland, the historical thriller stars anti-Communist Home Army insurgents in a doomed underground plot to resist Soviet rule. In his performance as militant Maciek, Zbigniew Cybulski approaches and at times surpasses the youthful, tragic cool of James Dean, while Jerzy Wójcik’s stark camerawork ignites an inflammatory script into Wajda’s fiercest unraveling of national myth and taboo. Overflowing with Christian symbolism, the film was the director’s proudest achievement; it remains to this day a widely discussed touchstone of the Polish Film School and one of modern cinema’s richest interrogations of agency and belief in the face of futility and (overwhelming, ambivalent) defeat. Part of the series Once There Was History . Andrzej Wajda at 100.

Linear Salsa is a hybrid dance that comes from Mambo (a Cuban style that was popularized in the 1950’s NYC Palladium). title: Jerry Bergonzi Quartet
description: $15 @ the door / $10 students / 8:30 start / 8pm doors / seated Jerry Bergonzi , Tenor Saxophone Luther Gray , Drums Plamen Karadonev, Piano Sean Farias, Bass Special Guest , Trumpet A fine, high-powered tenor saxophonist with a tone influenced by John Coltrane, a mastery of chord changes, and a strong musical imagination, Jerry Bergonzi has long had an underground following in the Boston area. He started on clarinet when he was eight, switching to alto at 12, and finally to tenor two years later. Bergonzi was inspired early on by Sonny Rollins, Coltrane, and Hank Mobley. He attended Lowell University and then after graduation played electric bass in local bands behind singers and strippers, saving up enough money to move to New York in 1972. After struggling in the Big Apple for seven years and gaining some recognition as a member of Two Generations of Brubeck and of the Dave Brubeck Quartet (with whom he appeared on several Concord albums during 1979-1981), Bergonzi moved back to Boston in 1981, where he developed a strong career both as a tenorman and as an educator. He has since led several groups (including two called Con Brio and Gonz) and recorded for the Plug, Not Fat, Red, and Blue Note labels. — By Scott Yanow, AllMusic Continuing Every Monday at 8:30pm Lineup subject to change

title: The Fringe
description: $15 @ the door / $10 students / 10pm doors / 10:30 start / seated The Fringe originally formed back in 1971 by tenor-saxophonist George Garzone , bassist Richard Appleman, and drummer Bob Gullotti as an outlet for their free jazz improvisations, The Fringe have entertained and enlightened Boston area jazz audiences for over 50 years. Bassist Appleman left the band in 1985 to become Chairman of the Bass Department at Berklee College and was replaced by veteran bassist John Lockwood . Bob Gullotti passed away in 2020 and is remembered as one of the greatest jazz drummers of his generation. Francisco Mela, now on drums, graciously fills the space Bob left behind. Along with their impressive tenure with The Fringe, Garzone, Lockwood, and Mela are in great demand as session players and have played with many of the greats of contemporary jazz. Along with keeping up with a busy performance schedule, each of them are well-respected educators helping to inspire the jazz musicians of tomorrow. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I am a dance artist, teacher and performer as well as a clinical social worker. description: Have you ever wondered what happens in our conservation labs? In this session, conservation technician Yi Bin Liang will give a demonstration of construction methods used to prepare objects for exhibition, such as making hinges, frames, and small enclosures. The Straus Center for Conservation and Technical Studies is a world leader in fine arts conservation, research, and training. The center’s laboratories are where conservation, conservation science, and curatorial practice intersect, coming together to enrich the understanding of and care for the approximately 250,000 objects in the Harvard Art Museums collections.

title: Wintery Songs in Eleventy Part Harmony at Club Passim
description: Wintery Songs in Eleventy Part Harmony is a loose collaboration of Boston-based musicians organized by veteran singer/songwriter Jennifer Kimball, who celebrate the holiday season with their delightful annual program of sacred, secular and wintery pop music rearranged, reharmonized, and often just plain turned on its head. Wielding fiddles, cellos, ukes, guitars and glockenspiels, this ensemble re-envisions the sounds of the season by reharmonizing classic songs, reinterpreting pop tunes, composing new songs for the season and bringing unknown pop gems to the lexicon of holiday-ish music. From Sinatra to Tchaikovsky, Isaac Watts to Ana Egge, this beautifully eclectic mix of sacred and secular music inspires a reinvention of the holiday experience; one where minor keys are as familiar as major, the church has transformed into a club where all are welcome and the season’s darkness is as deep as it’s festive lights are welcoming.

title: Intermediate/Advanced Ballet with Dean Vollick
description: Class begins with a thorough set of exercises at the barre that last from 30 to 45 minutes. Centre practice follows, and may consist of a battement tendu exercise, a battement jeté exercise, a grand battement exercise, small and/or large adage, stationary turns, traveling turns, and petite and grand allegro enchaînement (small and big jumps). Classes are structured so that the dancer warms up their feet, legs, hips and upper body gradually. As class progresses there are more changes of weight and eventually, sudden changes of direction. Live music is provided by a pianist, that ranges from classical pieces to selections from ballet repertoire to improvisational contemporary music. Ballet originated in the Italian Renaissance courts around 1500 as large balls or spectacles that were performed by members of the royal court. The French king, Louis XIV, created the first academy and the positions, steps, and movements of the ballet were collected and codified. The spectacles began to be performed by artists that were trained in the academy, originally as part of an opera, and later as ballets that told a story through music, mime, and dance. Over the centuries ballet has influenced folk dance styles of many (mainly European) nations and, more recently, has been influenced by folk, modern, and contemporary forms of dance from all countries. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? I had a professional dance career that spanned more than twenty years and included company work in both ballet and contemporary companies as well as dancing, choreographing, and teaching as a freelance artist.

description: Classes will be broken into 5 sections at Level 1. New sessions start the first Monday of every odd month. Warmup Footwork Review Foundational move for Level 1 On2 Linear Salsa (of which there are 7) Dance with Music Philosophically things to be on the lookout for, the importance of melding footwork and partner-work when dancing Salsa, the importance of spaced repetition, the importance of tying everything to Social dancing, and personal convolutional schemes to try to attenuate the lead/follow dichotomy. No partner required. *NEW* The Dance Complex requires ALL visitors to have a Membership, Guest Pass, or $5 Day Pass to access the building. *Students who purchase a membership for the Dance Complex will get that $25 taken off their 10 class new student rate, bringing it down to $85. Linear Salsa is a hybrid dance that comes from Mambo (a Cuban style that was popularized in the 1950’s NYC Palladium). NY Mambo is a marriage of footwork and partner-work from Cuba (Aftro-Cuban movements, Cuban Son) and the U.S. (Jazz, Swing). Salsa is a marketing term popularized in the 1970’s to commodify all Latin music and dance to a U.S. audience. Circular Salsa primarily comes from the Cuban dance Casino, which itself originates from Cuban Son. Salsa is by nature transformational, multinational, and multigenerational, embodying the shared heritage of Latin music. description: Wintery Songs in Eleventy Part Harmony is a loose collaboration of Boston-based musicians organized by veteran singer/songwriter Jennifer Kimball, who celebrate the holiday season with their delightful annual program of sacred, secular and wintery pop music rearranged, reharmonized, and often just plain turned on its head. Wielding fiddles, cellos, ukes, guitars and glockenspiels, this ensemble re-envisions the sounds of the season by reharmonizing classic songs, reinterpreting pop tunes, composing new songs for the season and bringing unknown pop gems to the lexicon of holiday-ish music. From Sinatra to Tchaikovsky, Isaac Watts to Ana Egge, this beautifully eclectic mix of sacred and secular music inspires a reinvention of the holiday experience; one where minor keys are as familiar as major, the church has transformed into a club where all are welcome and the season’s darkness is as deep as it’s festive lights are welcoming.

It’s based on the original exercises created by Joseph Pilates, and can be practiced on a mat with little to no equipment. What background, training, and or relationship do you have with this style/technique/class subject? Carolina started her journey teaching in 2020. Carolina’s certifications all align in how she teaches her classes that are mindful and invigorating. title: In-Person Bellydance
description: In this class, you’ll explore earthy Egyptian, Turkish, and American style movements, dynamic combinations, and expressive choreography blending tradition and innovation. Experience the power of fiery hip-locks and shimmies, and the fluid beauty of serpentine undulations. Instructions: Wear comfortable dance or workout clothing that allows you to move freely. Classes are danced barefoot or in dance shoes. The more authentic name for this dance form is raqs sharqi (“dance of the East”), and its roots lie in the Middle and Near East, primarily in Egypt and Turkey. This dance form was introduced to the United States and Europe at the turn of the 20th century, but it was not widely performed or taught until the 1950s and 1960s, when the belly dance craze swept across the U.S. The American cabaret style of belly dance is rooted in the legacy passed down by notable American teachers and performers, who blended Middle Eastern influences with their own innovations and movement styles drawn from diverse dance backgrounds. title: Wintery Songs in Eleventy Part Harmony at Club Passim
description: Wintery Songs in Eleventy Part Harmony is a loose collaboration of Boston-based musicians organized by veteran singer/songwriter Jennifer Kimball, who celebrate the holiday season with their delightful annual program of sacred, secular and wintery pop music rearranged, reharmonized, and often just plain turned on its head. Wielding fiddles, cellos, ukes, guitars and glockenspiels, this ensemble re-envisions the sounds of the season by reharmonizing classic songs, reinterpreting pop tunes, composing new songs for the season and bringing unknown pop gems to the lexicon of holiday-ish music. From Sinatra to Tchaikovsky, Isaac Watts to Ana Egge, this beautifully eclectic mix of sacred and secular music inspires a reinvention of the holiday experience; one where minor keys are as familiar as major, the church has transformed into a club where all are welcome and the season’s darkness is as deep as it’s festive lights are welcoming.
